summary: Research stylized rendering directions for Dig Down (3D ice world + 2D sprite hero) and synthesize distinct style options

research.angle: 2D sprites in 3D worlds (HD-2D, Paper Mario, Don't Starve, Cult of the Lamb, Hollow Knight, Dead Cells, Tidebreaker): why our puppy reads as a 'sticker between boxes' and what fixes it
key_insights: DIAGNOSIS 1, two lighting models (inferred, from reading src/main3d.ts:270). The world is MeshToonMaterial with a hard 3-step ramp. The hero is MeshLambertMaterial, which has smooth falloff. A smooth gradient on a flat plane beside banded cubes reads as 'from a different renderer'. The AI sprite also has painted highlights and shadows of its own, so it gets lit twice (once in the art, once by the scene) from directions that don't agree. HD-2D does the opposite: it starts from a 'deformed' drawing and 'builds up' realism with lighting on top (sourced: Triangle Strategy producers). A third-party HD-2D spec states it directly: 'drawn with neutral, baked-in-nothing lighting; the scene's lights and grading supply all mood' (sourced, but that is a GitHub issue, not Square Enix).

DIAGNOSIS 2, mixed dimensionality on the hero (inferred, from main3d.ts:255-318). The drill is a 3D primitive with its own inverted-hull ink, attached to a flat plane. The drill's real depth and parallax expose the sprite as paper. Everything on the character must share one dimensionality: draw the drill into the sprite frames, or make it a second flat card.

DIAGNOSIS 3, outlines that don't match (inferred). The blocks' ink is an inverted hull scaled about 1.12x, so its screen-pixel width changes with distance and perspective. The sprite's ink is baked into the image at whatever weight the AI tool chose, then shrunk with linear filtering and mipmaps, so it ends up thinner and softer. Don't Starve bakes ink into all its art and uses no outline shader (sourced, through a third-party breakdown). Either way, one ink rule has to cover everything.

DIAGNOSIS 4, mismatched detail and texel density (inferred, plus a sourced texel-density principle). The sprite is a dense illustration; the blocks are flat colors with a procedural frost texture. 'Players notice density mismatches more than absolute resolution' (sourced: Bitsoul texel density guide). An HD-2D reference spec says to pick one texels-per-unit and hold every texture to it (sourced, GitHub spec).

DIAGNOSIS 5, front view against side motion (inferred). The hero is a single front-facing pose that slides sideways and digs down. With no turn, dig pose or contact squash per action, it moves like a cut-out slid across a board. Tidebreaker's cohesion comes largely from full Spriterrific idle/walk/run/jump/hurt frames made from one reference (sourced: spriterrific.com).

DIAGNOSIS 6, the sprite doesn't sit inside the space (inferred). The plane sits at z=0.25 in front of a carved cell, and the contact shadow is the only cue that it's there. The dug cavity needs dark interior faces, ambient occlusion and a rim of light on the sprite, so it reads as being in a hole rather than pasted over one. Cult of the Lamb writes its 2D art to depth and rotates it toward the camera to use '3D world techniques' (sourced: Massive Monster on Steam).

PRINCIPLE (sourced: HD-2D Wikipedia, Asano). The cohesion comes from LIGHT, not from geometry: point lights make sprites cast shadows, plus DoF/tilt-shift, bloom and particles. Asano said the look took about a month and a half to dial in.

PRINCIPLE (sourced: Hollow Knight analyses). The layers are foreground, playable midground and background, and the player is usually the brightest light in dim areas. That fits a dark ice cave with a headlamp puppy.

PRINCIPLE (inferred). For Mr. Driller readability, the block-color layer must stay sharp, saturated and unblurred. All atmosphere (DoF, fog, bloom, parallax, aurora) lives in the sky, the shaft walls and the background, never on the 9 playable columns.

techniques.name: One shading model: put the sprite on the same toon ramp
techniques.what: Light the sprite with the same quantized N.L ramp and the same lights as the blocks, and strip baked lighting out of the sprite art (flat albedo, at most one painted ambient-occlusion tone).
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Removes the 'different renderer' look. The 3-band banding then shows on both the puppy and the ice cubes, and the headlamp, aurora and depth darkening hit both the same way.
techniques.threejs_how: Swap MeshLambertMaterial for MeshToonMaterial({map, gradientMap: ramp, alphaTest: 0.5, transparent: false}). A plain plane gets one uniform band, which is fine as a baseline. Better: feed a normal map (next technique) or pass a fake 'puffy' normal in onBeforeCompile so the left/right halves fall into different bands. Re-generate the AI sprite with prompts like 'flat colors, no shading, even lighting, cel shade only 1 shadow tone'.

techniques.name: Sprite normal maps (hand-made, generated, or baked from Tripo/Blender)
techniques.what: Give the flat sprite a per-pixel normal map so scene lights wrap around the head, hoodie and ears, as HD-2D, Dead Cells and modern sprite pipelines do.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The strongest single cue that makes a flat character feel volumetric in 3D light. The warm headlamp lights the face, and cold ice bounce from below lights the jaw.
techniques.threejs_how: MeshToonMaterial supports normalMap natively, so set normalMap and normalScale; with a toon ramp the result stays cel-banded. Three ways to get normals: (a) a Blender headless script that bakes normals from the Tripo puppy model rendered in an orthographic front view, the Dead Cells approach of rendering frames plus a normal map from 3D; (b) normals generated from the alpha distance field (blur the alpha, take its gradient as xy, z = 1) in a build script; (c) an AI normal-map tool. Keep normalScale low so the result reads as cel shading, not plastic.

techniques.name: Alpha-offset rim light (no normal map needed)
techniques.what: Sample the sprite's alpha shifted toward the light's screen direction. Where the shifted sample is transparent, you are on the lit edge, so add a rim color. Use cold aurora-cyan from above/behind and a warm rim from the headlamp side.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: A thin light edge separates the dark puppy from dark ice, keeps the hero readable deep in the cave, and makes it look lit by this world. A cheap, big win.
techniques.threejs_how: In onBeforeCompile on the sprite material (or in a small ShaderMaterial), compute uv + lightDirScreen * texelSize * N and take rim = (1 - texture(map, offsetUv).a) * alpha. Add rim * rimColor before tone mapping. Pass the light direction in screen space as a uniform from the CPU each frame. One extra texture tap per fragment.

techniques.name: One ink rule: screen-space outline pass OR ink drawn into everything
techniques.what: Pick a single outline system with a constant screen-pixel width for both blocks and hero. Option A: a post-process edge detection on depth and normals over the whole scene, sprite included because it writes depth. Option B: drop the inverted hulls and draw ink into all textures: block faces get an inked border texture, and the sprite gets ink at the same pixel weight.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Matching line weight is the number-one cohesion cue in flat-cartoon styles. It also improves block-chunk readability, because a depth edge appears exactly where chunks of different colors meet.
techniques.threejs_how: Option A: RenderPixelatedPass (three/addons) already does depth- and normal-edge outlines with normalEdgeStrength/depthEdgeStrength, which suits pixel mode. For non-pixel mode, use a custom ShaderPass reading a depth texture plus a normal render target (Omar Shehata's method), kernel up/down/left/right only. Add a color-ID edge as well: write the block color index to a channel so same-color merged chunks get no inner edge. Option B: a 2-line frost-border texture on the merged-chunk faces, and generate sprite frames at a fixed ink width relative to the target on-screen height (for example, ask the AI for a 3px line at final size, then nearest-downscale).

techniques.name: Grounding kit: camera-plane alignment, foot pivot, alpha shadow, blob shadow, cavity AO
techniques.what: Keep the sprite aligned to the camera plane (rotation = camera rotation, not lookAt), pivoted at the feet. Have it cast a real alpha-cut shadow onto the cavity floor, and also draw a soft blob shadow that shrinks when the hero hops or falls. Carve the dug cell as a visible cavity with darker toon-ramp side faces and an occlusion gradient, and let the front lip of the block above slightly overlap the sprite's top.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Contact, occlusion and cast shadow are what make 'in the hole' read instead of 'on the glass'. Blob shadows are also gameplay-readable: they show where you'll land and that blocks above are falling.
techniques.threejs_how: Already done: quaternion copy and customDepthMaterial with alphaTest. Add: the blob as a radial-gradient texture on a quad (better than a hard circle), scale it by 1 - hopY. Give the cavity explicit inner wall meshes (an instanced inset box per dug cell) with vertex-color AO toward the corners. Keep the sprite on alphaTest (opaque pass, writes depth) so it sorts against blocks; the Spriterrific Three.js guide suggests depthWrite:false with transparency, which is fine for floating FX but loses sorting. Optional: render falling blocks' shadows on the hero.

techniques.name: Texel-density lock (and pixel-grid lock in pixel mode)
techniques.what: Fix one texels-per-world-unit, for example 32 or 48 px per block cell, and author everything to it: sprite frames, block face textures, frost, particles. In pixel mode, author the sprite at exactly the on-screen pixel size, snap the camera to the texel grid, and nearest-upscale.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This kills the 'HD illustration pasted on low-detail cubes' look. Pixel art on a 3D world reads as one image only when both share a pixel grid, which is HD-2D's core trick and also David Holland's.
techniques.threejs_how: Hero ~1.2 cells tall at 48 px per cell gives a ~58 px-tall sprite: generate at high res, then quantize with nearest downscale and palette reduction in a Node/sharp or Python script. Set texture filters to NearestFilter with no mipmaps for pixel styles. Camera snapping: round the camera position to the world size of one render pixel, then offset the upscaled canvas by the sub-pixel remainder (David Holland's method). Render-target size = lines / devicePixelRatio as now.

techniques.name: Diorama post stack: depth-masked tilt-shift, selective bloom, grade, vignette
techniques.what: HD-2D's signature: blur the top and bottom of the frame (tilt-shift), bloom only on bright sources, then color grading and vignette. For us, blur only beyond the playfield (sky and aurora on the surface, far cave background, outer shaft walls), bloom only on emissive things (aurora, stars, ice crystals, air capsules, headlamp halo), and apply a cold LUT that darkens with depth.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The miniature, toy-box effect gives instant cohesion and 'premium' feel. Keeping blur off the 9 columns preserves gameplay readability.
techniques.threejs_how: EffectComposer: RenderPass, then a custom single-pass tilt-shift that uses the depth texture to mask blur (or HorizontalTiltShiftShader plus VerticalTiltShiftShader from three/addons/shaders at half resolution), then UnrealBloomPass with a high threshold so only emissive and HDR pixels bloom, then OutputPass with a 3D LUT (LUTPass) and vignette folded into the same final shader. Mobile: 2-tier quality. Low tier = bloom at quarter resolution, no DoF, and a cheap vignette and gradient in the final pass. BokehPass is too heavy for mobile; prefer separable Gaussian blur at half resolution.

techniques.name: Light as the mood engine: the hero is the brightest light, with a cookie and depth falloff
techniques.what: As you go deeper, ambient and sun light drop and the puppy's warm headlamp becomes the key light. Add a light cookie (a projected texture) for the headlamp beam, and give blocks a minimum readable floor brightness so their colors never go muddy. The aurora tints only the top 2-3 rows near the surface.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This gives the hero visual priority without making him bigger, and turns 'getting darker as you dig' into felt atmosphere. Warm/cold contrast (amber lamp on blue ice) is the same color story that makes Tidebreaker cohesive (warm lamp, cold night).
techniques.threejs_how: A SpotLight with spot.map (three.js supports projected textures on SpotLight) plus the existing PointLight. On the block material, use onBeforeCompile to add a clamp: outgoingLight = max(outgoingLight, albedo * floor). Drive hemi/sun/fog per level as now, and animate the aurora as a cheap emissive shader plane in the sky. Use at most 2-3 dynamic lights for mobile, and keep shadow mapSize at 1024 or move to 512 on the low tier.

techniques.name: Parallax layers and foreground silhouettes around the shaft
techniques.what: Use three layers like Hollow Knight. Background: painted AI ice-cave cards at 2-3 depths, fogged and blurred. Midground: the 9-column playfield. Foreground: dark icicle and crystal silhouettes at the screen edges that pass the camera faster than the playfield.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Gives the world more detail than the sprite carries, which is the 2.5D balance HD-2D and Hollow Knight strike. The sprite stops being the only drawn-looking thing, so it no longer looks foreign.
techniques.threejs_how: Stack textured planes at different z values (true perspective parallax for free) with MeshBasicMaterial and fog. Generate the cards with ChatGPT image in the same ink and palette rules, using alphaTest for silhouettes. Keep each one under 1024 px, atlas them, and recycle a few cards vertically as the camera descends.

references.title: The Art of Hollow Knight (foreground/midground/background layers, blur, particles)
PC Gamer: Hollow Knight art

techniques.name: Make the flat hero move like a drawing: poses plus vertex deformation
techniques.what: Generate proper frames (side walk, dig down, dig sideways, idle breathing, crushed, out of air) and add Spine-like mesh deformation in the vertex shader: bend, squash and ear or hoodie wobble. Use split head and body cards so the head bobs independently.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: A single front-view card sliding sideways is the 'sticker' look. Deformation plus pose changes make him read as a living paper character, as in Cult of the Lamb, Paper Mario and Don't Starve.
techniques.threejs_how: Get a spritesheet from Spriterrific or ChatGPT image using the single reference, and play it with texture.offset/repeat UV animation. Subdivide the PlaneGeometry (for example 4x8) and in the vertex shader apply a sin-based bend weighted by uv.y, plus squash driven by the existing hop/land values. Separate head and body planes, a couple of mm apart, with their own pivots. Flip with negative scale.x (already done; works on a mesh, which is why Spriterrific recommends PlaneGeometry over THREE.Sprite).

exemplar_games.game: Octopath Traveler / Triangle Strategy / Live A Live (HD-2D)
exemplar_games.what_to_steal: Neutral, deformed pixel sprites with the scene's realistic light layered on top. Point-light sprite shadows, tilt-shift DoF, bloom only on bright sources, a strong grade. The look comes from the light and post stack, not from the geometry.
Sprites aligned to the camera plane under a fixed angled camera, alpha clip that writes depth, ink baked into all art (world and characters alike), blob shadows, separate head and body transforms.

2D art that writes to depth and is rotated toward the camera, Spine mesh deformation, and a dedicated lighting pass as the main cohesion tool. Cute and creepy tonal contrast through light, not detail.

Render a 3D model (our Tripo puppy) at tiny size without anti-aliasing into sprite frames plus normal maps, then shade with a toon shader. That gives animation frames and normals from one model through a Blender headless script.
Foreground, midground and background layers with blur and particles. Dim areas where the player is the brightest light. A painterly world carrying more detail than the character.

Same toolchain as ours (GPT images, Blender + Tripo, Spriterrific, an AI coding agent). Proof that a full animation set, a small sprite and a dark scene with warm/cold lamp light hold together. Our version: an amber headlamp against blue ice and aurora.

style_direction_ideas: A. 'Ice Diorama HD-2D' (pixel): pixel-art puppy at about 58 px tall on a locked 48 px-per-cell grid. World rendered at 480 lines through RenderPixelatedPass (depth and normal edges give a uniform 1-px ink). Toon blocks with 2-3 bands, camera texel snapping, a tilt-shift band only on the sky and the deep background, selective bloom on aurora and air capsules, a cold LUT that darkens per 100 m, amber headlamp cookie. Closest to Octopath, and the best mobile fit.

B. 'Ink Cel 2.5D' (flat cartoon, Don't Starve / Cult of the Lamb): keep the 3D toon cubes, but replace the inverted hulls with one screen-space ink pass (plus color-ID edges for chunk borders) so the line width matches the sprite's baked 3-px ink. Re-generate the puppy flat-lit with one shadow tone, add an alpha-offset rim light (cyan aurora and warm lamp), subdivided-plane wobble, split head and body. Painted parallax cave cards and foreground icicle silhouettes.

C. 'Paper Diorama' (Paper Mario): commit to cardboard instead of fighting it. Blocks become thick cut-cardstock ice tiles with a beveled paper edge and grain, the hero is an obviously paper cut-out with a white die-cut border, paper-flip turns and a cast shadow on the cavity floor. Uniform warm studio light plus aurora. The 'sticker' becomes the intended aesthetic.

D. 'Flat Stage, 3D Light' (Sea of Stars / xDasher-like): drop perspective for an orthographic, nearly frontal camera so cubes stop showing side faces next to a flat hero. Blocks become front-face tiles with normal maps (beveled ice) in the same pixel density as the sprite, all lit by real dynamic lights (headlamp, crystal glow) with normal-mapped sprites. Maximum readability, and the 2D and 3D mismatch disappears by construction.

research.angle: Stylized/NPR 3D rendering in Three.js: how to make a toon-shaded 3D ice shaft and a flat-cartoon (or pixel) 2D Yorkie sprite read as one illustrated image, with concrete passes and shaders and their mobile cost.
key_insights: (inferred) The mismatch most likely comes from the world and the hero following different drawing rules, not from too few effects. The hero sprite has screen-constant bold black lines, flat fills and no lighting falloff. The world has inverted-hull lines whose width changes with perspective and depth, a 3-step ramp, ACES tone mapping and fog. To fix it, make the world obey the sprite's rules: the same outline width in screen pixels, the same number of tone steps, the same shadow hue and the same palette. Then run one final pass over both so they share grain and color grading.

(sourced + inferred) Screen-space edge detection on depth plus normals or IDs gives outlines of constant pixel width. That matches a hand-drawn sprite outline better than an inverted hull, whose thickness is in world units. Maxime Heckel's Moebius post combines both gradients (gradientDepth*25 + gradientNormal), and Omar Shehata's webgl-outlines repo shows a Three.js version with an FXAA pass after it.

(inferred, high value for gameplay) Detect edges on a CHUNK ID instead of normals. Write each block's chunk ID (one per merged same-color group) into an ID buffer, then draw a thick line wherever the ID changes. That gives one bold outline around each merged chunk and no seams inside it, which is exactly the shape the player has to read, and the hero can write its own ID to get a matching line. This follows Omar Shehata's surface-ID outline method (sourced), applied to puzzle semantics.

(sourced) Sable (Shedworks) improved readability in a flat-shaded world by adding shadows so characters sit on surfaces, using distance fog they called 'really, really key', and fading outline opacity with distance. In our shaft, fading line and color contrast with depth below the play window would push background ice back while active blocks stay crisp.

(sourced) Hi-Fi Rush, per GDC 2024 notes, keeps visuals 'clean sharp bright'. It uses halftone dots in lit areas and hatching in shadow, applied in model or world space rather than stuck to the camera, and colors shadows through a world-space volume instead of using plain black. Takeaway: a pattern overlay should move with the surface, and shadows should be tinted (deep blue-violet for ice), not darkened toward black.

(sourced) Dead Cells renders 3D models tiny with no antialiasing, plus a normal map and a basic toon shader, to get pixel-art frames. A Short Hike renders at low resolution, scales up, and uses flat cohesive shading with a soft outline for readability. t3ssel8r-style renderers guarantee 1-pixel outlines at low internal resolution, add highlights only on convex edges, and snap the camera to a texel grid to stop shimmer. This is the proven route if the user picks pixel art.

(inferred) Ortho vs perspective: a near-frontal perspective camera makes outer columns show side faces and pulls the shaft into a vanishing point, which clashes with a flat front-view sprite. An OrthographicCamera, or a very narrow FOV (around 10-15 deg) pulled far back, keeps blocks reading as flat tiles with a small hint of depth and matches the sprite's projection.

(inferred) Mobile budget: most stylization should happen in the materials, which cost nothing extra. Keep post-processing to ONE merged full-screen pass (outline + grade + grain + vignette) at a capped pixel ratio. The pmndrs/postprocessing EffectPass merges effects into a single shader and draws with a single full-screen triangle (sourced). Avoid the three/examples OutlinePass for whole-scene lines: it is built for selection highlights, and users report it slowing on dense meshes and misbehaving on iOS (sourced, three.js issues and forum).

techniques.name: Screen-space ID/depth edge outline (replace inverted hull)
techniques.what: Render the scene once into a target that also stores an ID (chunk ID per merged block group, hero ID, background ID) and depth. Run a small cross or Sobel kernel in post-processing and draw a dark line where the ID changes or depth jumps. Line width is set in screen pixels.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Gives one bold outline per merged chunk, with the same weight as the sprite's drawn outline, at every column and depth. Chunk shapes become the strongest graphic element. It also removes the inverted hull's doubled-up and perspective-thinned lines, and the extra instanced draw.
techniques.threejs_how: WebGL2 multiple render targets: new THREE.WebGLRenderTarget(w,h,{count:2, depthTexture:new THREE.DepthTexture()}). Patch the block material with onBeforeCompile so it writes the chunk ID (an instanced attribute encoded to RGB) into the second output (layout(location=1)). Then a full-screen ShaderMaterial or a pmndrs postprocessing Effect samples the ID at 4 neighbors times thickness and mixes in the ink color. Inner crease lines can come from a normal or depth term at lower weight. Fallback without MRT: a second pass with scene.overrideMaterial set to an ID material, which is cheap because blocks are instanced.

techniques.name: Hard 2-tone cel shading with hue-shifted shadow and rim light (custom toon ShaderMaterial)
techniques.what: Replace the 3-step MeshToonMaterial ramp with 2 tones: a lit color and a shadow color shifted in hue (cooler and more saturated for ice, not just darker). Add a thin rim band on the light-facing silhouette and a small hard specular dot, which suits ice. Tone edges use a smoothstep over about 0.01.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: A flat cartoon sprite has 1-2 tones per color. Matching that count is the single biggest step toward cohesion. Hue-shifted shadows keep the 4 block colors distinct even in shadow, so gameplay readability survives dark depths.
techniques.threejs_how: Either MeshToonMaterial with a 2-texel DataTexture gradientMap (NearestFilter required), plus onBeforeCompile to inject the rim and shadow-tint uniforms, or a ShaderMaterial with lights:true and UniformsLib.lights so it still receives the directional shadow map. Rim formula from Roystan/Maya Ndljk: rim = smoothstep(a-0.01, a+0.01, (1-dot(V,N)) * pow(NdotL, t)). Per-color shadow tint lives in a small uniform array indexed by the instance color ID.

techniques.name: Unified palette via gradient map / 3D LUT final grade
techniques.what: Grade the whole frame, sprite and 3D together, through one color LUT authored for the ice-night mood: cold blue shadows, cyan midtones, warm headlamp highlights. Optionally quantize to a fixed palette of about 16-32 colors.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: AI-generated sprite colors and procedurally lit block colors start out in different color spaces and moods. One final grade forces them onto one palette, which is a cheap and very effective way to make them cohere. Swapping the LUT per 100 m level (surface aurora, then deep cave) changes the mood with no new art.
techniques.threejs_how: three/addons/postprocessing/LUTPass.js with LUTCubeLoader (.cube files from Photoshop or Resolve), or pmndrs LUT3DEffect merged into the single EffectPass. Consider replacing ACES with NoToneMapping or Neutral plus the LUT, since ACES desaturates and shifts flat brand colors (inferred). For pixel mode, add a nearest-palette lookup in the same shader.

techniques.name: Paper / crayon grain overlay with world-locked texture
techniques.what: Multiply a paper-fiber or crayon-tooth texture over the final image at low opacity, and optionally use it to break up line edges (wobble the outline sample UV slightly with noise).
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The cheapest way to make the 3D world look like the same medium as a drawn sprite. Lock the paper to the shaft (scroll it with camera Y) rather than to the screen, so it does not look like a dirty lens. That follows Hi-Fi Rush's rule that patterns should not appear painted onto the camera.
techniques.threejs_how: Add one texture sample in the merged final pass: uv = screenUV*scale + vec2(0, cameraY*k). Hand-drawn line wobble, from Heckel: offset the edge-sample UV by vec2(sin(fragCoord.y*f), cos(fragCoord.x*f))*amp plus a hash. Generate the paper texture with ChatGPT image as a tileable 512px grayscale image.

techniques.name: Halftone in light / hatching in shadow (comic shader)
techniques.what: In the block material, overlay a halftone dot pattern on lit faces and diagonal hatch lines in shadow. Pattern density follows luminance, and the pattern is computed per block face in UV space so it moves with falling blocks.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Adds an illustrated, comic-book texture that suits a cartoon hero. Hatching density can also encode danger: denser hatching on X-blocks, or on a chunk that is wobbling and about to fall (inferred gameplay use).
techniques.threejs_how: In the toon ShaderMaterial, compute an SDF for dots and lines from the block UV (fract(uv*N)) with smoothstep antialiasing, as Hi-Fi Rush did. Threshold it with NdotL and shadow. No extra passes. Heckel's version uses mod(uv*res, 8) stripes at luma thresholds.

techniques.name: Low-res pixel pipeline with 1px ID outlines, convex highlights and camera snap
techniques.what: Render at a fixed low internal resolution (for example 270-360 lines), with no antialiasing and nearest-filter upscale. Draw 1-pixel outlines from the ID/depth edges, add a 1-pixel bright highlight on convex block edges (top-left ice glint), and snap the camera to the texel grid while adding the sub-texel remainder back in screen space.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: If the user picks the pixel art hero, this makes the 3D blocks look hand-pixeled at the same scale as the sprite. Without camera snapping, the vertical scrolling shaft would shimmer badly.
techniques.threejs_how: Render to a WebGLRenderTarget sized to the internal resolution (NearestFilter), run the edge and highlight pass at that resolution, then blit to the canvas with nearest filtering. Snap: round the camera position to world-units-per-texel, then offset the final blit by the fractional error. The hero sprite should be authored at the same texel density and positions rounded to whole texels. This is cheaper than full resolution on mobile because fill rate drops.

techniques.name: Depth-staged fog, outline fade and value hierarchy
techniques.what: Three value layers. Active play columns get full contrast with black lines. Shaft walls and background ice get lighter, color-tinted lines and fog toward a deep blue. The sky and aurora get no lines. Fade outline opacity and contrast by view depth and by distance below the hero.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Keeps falling and wobbling blocks the highest-contrast thing on screen while the world adds mood. This is the readability fix Sable credits to fog and outline fading.
techniques.threejs_how: In the outline pass, compute lineAlpha = 1 - smoothstep(near, far, linearDepth) and tint the line color toward the fog color. Use scene.fog or FogExp2 on background materials only, and skip it on active blocks (fog:false), so gameplay blocks are never fogged.

techniques.name: Painterly Kuwahara filter (backgrounds only)
techniques.what: An edge-preserving smoothing filter that turns renders into brush-stroke patches. There are box (4-sector), circular (8-sector, Papari) and anisotropic variants.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It can make AI- or Tripo-sourced background art (surface village, ice caverns) look painted and hide mismatched texture detail. On gameplay blocks it would blur chunk edges and hurt readability, so limit it to a pre-rendered or static background layer (inferred).
techniques.threejs_how: Bake it offline: run Kuwahara once on background images (or in Blender compositing) and ship the results as textures, so the runtime cost is zero. Runtime option: pmndrs/react-postprocessing has a Kuwahara effect, and threejs-blocks has a WebGPU painterly example, but the nested-loop sampling is heavy per pixel. Heckel notes Gaussian weighting is 'quite expensive' and swaps in polynomial weights.

techniques.name: Hero integration: outlined, rim-lit, palette-matched billboard
techniques.what: Treat the sprite as part of the world. It writes its own ID into the outline buffer so it gets the same ink line, receives the headlamp and ambient as a 2-tone (normal-map toon or simple tint) plus the same rim color, and goes through the same LUT and grain. Also redraw the sprite flat, with no painted shading, so the engine supplies the light.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: A pre-shaded illustration lit a second time by the scene looks pasted on. A flat-fill sprite plus engine-supplied 2-tone and rim lighting matches the blocks. Dead Cells used per-frame normal maps with a basic toon shader for exactly this reason.
techniques.threejs_how: Give the sprite a ShaderMaterial with an alphaTest cutout and an optional normal map (generate one with an AI tool or from the Tripo model rendered in Blender), using the same toon function as the blocks. Write the hero ID to MRT attachment 1. Keep the contact shadow as a hard-edged ellipse in the shadow color, not soft black.

exemplar_games.what_to_steal: Thin outlines plus flat soft tones with almost no shading, readability recovered through shadows, distance fog and outline fade with distance. A model for a calm, wide snowy surface above the shaft.

Clean, sharp, bright direction: halftone in light and hatching in shadow, applied on surfaces, tinted shadow colors from a world volume, and art-placed light volumes instead of physical lights. Matches the energetic cartoon hero.
The mindset: 3D built purely to imitate 2D, with every shader and model decision judged on the final 2D frame. The GDC 2015 talk is worth watching before tuning the toon threshold and lines.
Render 3D tiny with no antialiasing to get pixel frames, plus normal maps with a basic toon shader. A route to animating the Yorkie: Tripo model, rig in Blender, render pixel frames with normals.
Low internal resolution scaled up, flat cohesive shading and a soft outline so things stay readable with few pixels. Proof that a cozy snowy world works well at low resolution.

exemplar_games.game: t3ssel8r-style 3D pixel art (Unity prototypes, documented by David Holland)
exemplar_games.what_to_steal: Pixel-perfect 1px ID/depth outlines, highlights only on convex edges, and texel-grid camera snapping with sub-pixel compensation, needed for a smoothly scrolling shaft in pixel mode.

style_direction_ideas: A. 'Ink and Gouache Storybook' (flat cartoon hero): orthographic or narrow-FOV camera; 2-tone hue-shifted toon blocks; chunk-ID screen-space outlines about 3-4 px in a warm near-black that match the sprite's line weight; tileable paper grain locked to the shaft; one LUT per depth band (aurora violet at the surface, then teal, then deep indigo); outlines fade on background ice. Post cost: one MRT scene pass plus one merged pass. Safest high-cohesion option.

B. 'Frost Hi-Bit' (pixel art hero): 320-360 line internal render; 1px ID outlines; 1px convex ice glints on block top-left edges; 16-24 color palette quantization with ordered dithering on the aurora and fog gradients; texel-snapped camera; the hero drawn at the same texel density. Cheapest on mobile because fill rate is low, and very cohesive if the sprite's pixel scale matches.

C. 'Comic Night Shift' (Hi-Fi Rush flavor): bright saturated block colors, halftone dots on lit faces, cross-hatching in shadow that gets denser with depth, the warm headlamp as a hard-edged light pool, bold black lines, and impact frames (white flash with radial speed lines) on chunk pops and chains. Highest energy, but keep the patterns off gameplay-critical color areas or use them at low contrast.

D. 'Moebius Polar' (Sable flavor): thin lines, almost no shading, soft pastel ice palette, long fog falloff, and hatching only in deep shadow. Calm, premium mood for the surface and early levels. It needs extra readability help, such as a stronger chunk outline weight on active blocks, because low shading contrast can blur color identity.

research.angle: Pixel-art 3D rendering: a Three.js 3D shaft and a pixel-art hero drawn on one low-res pixel grid, with no shimmer, 1px outlines, a limited palette, and stepped lighting. Mr. Driller-level readability is the hard constraint.
key_insights: Camera grid snapping only fully fixes pixel creep under ORTHOGRAPHIC projection. Under perspective, pixels at different depths drift at different rates, so one snap cannot correct them all (sourced: Texel Splatting paper, arxiv 2603.14587, which also quotes ProPixelizer: 'pixel creep can only ever be solved for orthographic projections'). Our current nearly-frontal perspective camera is the main reason pixel mode looks unstable. Recommendation (inferred): switch to an OrthographicCamera, frontal or tilted a few degrees. Mr. Driller is a 2D grid anyway, so we lose almost nothing.

The official three.js example webgl_postprocessing_pixel.html (Kody King) already shows most of the pipeline we need: an OrthographicCamera, RenderPixelatedPass (pixel size, depth and normal edge strengths, NearestFilter targets), pixelAlignFrustum for panning, and pixelAlignObject that snaps moving objects to the screen pixel grid and restores their true transform after rendering (sourced: I read the example source on GitHub).

Outlines must be generated AT the internal resolution, so each kernel step is exactly one output pixel and every edge is 1px at any screen size (sourced: bababuyyy unity-isometric-pixel-pipeline README; davidhol.land article). Our inverted-hull outlines change thickness with distance and pixelate unevenly, so they should be replaced in pixel mode (inferred).

t3ssel8r-style smooth motion = snap the camera to a view-aligned texel grid, then shift the final image back in screen space by the snap error. You get smooth scrolling without pixel swimming (sourced: davidhol.land; bababuyyy README '_PixelPanOffset'). Our camera mostly scrolls vertically, which makes this cheap and very effective (inferred).

One shared pixel grid for the hero means: the hero's sprite texels map 1:1 to internal-render texels (quad size = spritePx / pixelsPerWorldUnit), its texture uses NearestFilter with no mipmaps, it is rendered INTO the same low-res target as the blocks, and its position is snapped to the texel grid every frame (inferred, built on the three.js example's pixelAlignObject plus pixelTexture helper, sourced). A sprite drawn at a different density from the world is the classic 'pasted-on' look the user is reacting to.

Dead Cells solved 'no animation frames' by building 3D models, rendering each frame very small 'without smoothing', and exporting a normal map per frame so a simple toon shader lights the sprite in-game. Characters were about 50px tall, animation ran at 30fps from few keyframes plus interpolation (sourced: sudonull translation of Thomas Vasseur's Gamasutra deep dive). That maps directly onto our Tripo + Blender headless toolchain for the Yorkie hero (inferred).

A Short Hike chose 'flat cohesive shading and no anti-aliasing' and 'added a soft outline effect to objects to help them stand out, and stay readable' with few pixels. It also ships a pixel-size option (sourced: PlayStation Blog). Takeaway: at low resolution, readability comes from flat shading plus outlines, not from texture detail.

Dithering reads best when dither dots map 1:1 to output pixels, and screen-space dither shimmers when the camera moves. Obra Dinn pinned the pattern to camera rotation, but it cannot be pinned during translation (sourced: Obra Dinn devlog summaries via setsideb / dukope TIG posts). Because our camera only translates in snapped texel steps, a screen-space Bayer pattern indexed by snapped world texel coordinates stays stable (inferred).

Gameplay readability rule (inferred): keep the 4 block hues OUT of the environment palette and never dither the blocks themselves. Reserve dithering for light falloff, fog and sky gradients. Outline chunks by color-ID change rather than by geometry, so merged same-color chunks read as one shape.

HD-2D (Octopath) pairs billboarded pixel sprites that cast proper shadows with a modern post stack: tilt-shift DoF, bloom only on bright light sources, light volumetric fog, grading and vignette (sourced: Wikipedia HD-2D and UE spotlight search summary; the UE page itself returned 403, so treat details as secondary-sourced).

techniques.name: Orthographic camera + integer-scaled low-res render target
techniques.what: Render the whole scene (blocks, hero, particles) into a small WebGLRenderTarget, e.g. 1 block = 16 or 24 internal px, then upscale to the canvas. Use an OrthographicCamera so all depths share one pixel grid.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is the foundation that makes all the other techniques work. Ortho lets snapping fully eliminate creep, so our perspective camera cannot stay. Tying block size to an integer pixel count makes every block exactly N px wide, which looks crisp and is very readable.
techniques.threejs_how: THREE.OrthographicCamera sized so the frustum width = 9 columns + margins in world units, with pixelsPerUnit = 16 (or 24). Compute internalW = floor(canvasW / scale), with the integer scale chosen from devicePixelRatio and screen size. Render to a WebGLRenderTarget(internalW, internalH) using NearestFilter and no MSAA, then draw a fullscreen quad. RenderPixelatedPass from three/addons/postprocessing can be the starting point, but write our own pass so we control outlines and IDs. Keep the camera tilt at 0 to 10 degrees, or fake depth with a slight oblique shear in the projection matrix. Set renderer antialias:false.

techniques.name: Snap-then-offset smooth pixel camera (t3ssel8r method)
techniques.what: Each frame, snap the camera position to the texel grid in view space, render, then offset the upscaled image by the fractional snap error so motion stays smooth while texels never swim.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The shaft scrolls constantly as the hero digs. Without this, every block edge crawls and flickers during scrolling. With plain snapping alone, scrolling looks steppy at low resolution.
techniques.threejs_how: texel = frustumHeight / internalH. snapped = round(cam.y / texel) * texel, err = cam.y - snapped. Render into a target 2 texels larger than the view (one texel of margin per side). In the upscale ShaderMaterial, sample with uv + vec2(errX, errY) / texelSize / targetSize. Restore the true camera position after render, as the three.js example does. Do the same for X if horizontal shake is added. Vertical-only scrolling makes the math trivial.

techniques.name: Sharp (anti-aliased) pixel upscale filter
techniques.what: Replace image-rendering: pixelated with a shader upscale that keeps texels hard but blends a sub-pixel band at texel borders using fwidth + smoothstep.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Mobile screens rarely divide evenly by our internal resolution. Nearest upscaling at non-integer ratios gives uneven pixel widths, which makes 1px outlines look 1 or 2px wide at random. A sharp filter keeps pixels uniform at any ratio and also hides the sub-pixel camera offset.
techniques.threejs_how: Fullscreen ShaderMaterial: vec2 px = uv * texSize; vec2 f = fract(px); vec2 w = fwidth(px); f = smoothstep(0.5 - w*0.5, 0.5 + w*0.5, f); sample at (floor(px) + f) / texSize with a LINEAR-filtered copy of the target. This is one extra texture sample per screen pixel. Note: the snippet is my reconstruction of the fwidth+smoothstep idea, which the repo only describes in prose.

techniques.name: 1px outlines from color-ID + depth at internal resolution (chunk-aware)
techniques.what: Write a per-pixel 'chunk/color ID' (plus depth) alongside color, and in the composite pass darken any pixel whose 4-neighbor ID or depth differs. Optionally lighten crease pixels (t3ssel8r-style highlight edges).
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This makes outlines exactly 1px everywhere and draws them around merged same-color CHUNKS, not around each cube, so the merge read becomes automatic. It also gives the hero sprite the same 1px outline, which binds it to the world. Darkened-neighbor colored lines (not pure black) look more like hand-pixeled art.
techniques.threejs_how: WebGL2 MRT: new WebGLRenderTarget(w, h, {count: 2}). Location 1 gets the ID from the instanced block material via onBeforeCompile (instance attribute colorId and chunkId) and gets the alpha mask for the hero. Alternatively, pack the ID into the alpha channel of the beauty target to avoid MRT. The edge shader samples 4 neighbors; if id != idN, output mix(color, color * 0.45, 1.0). Use a depth discontinuity for the hero and falling blocks against the background. RenderPixelatedPass's depthEdgeIndicator and normalEdgeIndicator code is a ready reference. Remove inverted-hull meshes in this mode, which also halves block draw cost.

techniques.name: Hero on the same pixel grid (texel-matched billboard)
techniques.what: Author the Yorkie sprite at the world's density (e.g. about 1.25 blocks tall = 20-30 px), render it into the same low-res target, and snap its position to texels each frame. Do squash, lean and hop as discrete per-frame poses or integer-pixel offsets, not continuous scaling.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is the single biggest fix for the 'awkward / pasted-on' feeling. Right now a high-res sprite sits in a differently-sampled world. Continuous squash on a pixel sprite produces mixed pixel sizes, so it should be quantized.
techniques.threejs_how: PlaneGeometry(spriteW / ppu, spriteH / ppu), texture.minFilter = magFilter = NearestFilter, generateMipmaps = false. Use alphaTest 0.5 (hard cutout, no semi-transparent fringe). Each frame: round position to texel / ppu in camera space (like the example's pixelAlignObject), render, restore. Quantize squash scale to steps that land on whole pixels (e.g. +/-1-2 px height). Downscale the chosen ChatGPT pixel-art candidate to the exact target size, cleaning by hand or with an indexed-palette reduction. Do not let the GPU minify it.

techniques.name: Dead Cells pipeline for hero animation: Tripo model -> Blender low-res frames + normal maps
techniques.what: Turn the hero into a 3D model (Tripo from the front-view art), rig and animate it in Blender, and batch-render each frame at sprite size with no anti-aliasing and flat/toon shading. Export a matching normal-map frame so the sprite responds to in-game lights.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This solves 'no animation frames yet' (dig left/right/down, fall, crushed, air-low panic) without hand-drawing, while staying consistent across frames. The normal maps let the headlamp, aurora and cave light wrap the Yorkie like the 3D blocks, the way Dead Cells lights its sprites with a simple toon shader.
techniques.threejs_how: Blender headless (bpy): orthographic camera, resolution = sprite px, film filter size about 0 or Workbench with AA off. Render a color pass + normal pass (or a Workbench 'normal' matcap), pack frames into a spritesheet atlas. In Three.js use a custom ShaderMaterial (or MeshToonMaterial with normalMap and an offset-repeat atlas) that does N·L against the headlamp and directional light, quantized into 2-3 bands. Sprite UV frame stepping at 12-15 fps for a chunky pixel feel. A fallback for normal maps from the 2D sprite alone is Laigter / Sprite Illuminator-style generation (see the arxiv survey).

techniques.name: Palette lock via LUT quantization
techniques.what: After lighting, map every output pixel to a fixed curated palette (e.g. 24-40 colors: ice blues, aurora greens/magentas, night navy, warm lamp amber, plus 4 reserved block hues with 3 tones each).
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Palette lock is what makes 3D read as 'pixel art' rather than 'blurry low-res 3D'. It also enforces cohesion between hero, blocks and background (the Tidebreaker-like unity the user misses). Reserved block hues guarantee readability.
techniques.threejs_how: Final composite ShaderMaterial does a 3D LUT lookup: bake a 32^3 or 16^3 nearest-palette LUT as a 2D strip texture (NearestFilter) offline in a Node script from a .hex palette, then index it with color.rgb. Alternatively, three/addons LUTPass with a nearest-palette .cube. Keep ACES tone mapping BEFORE quantization, or drop it and author the palette directly. Run the pass at internal resolution, so it is nearly free.

references.title: The Art of Dithering and Retro Shading for the Web (Maxime Heckel)

techniques.name: Stable ordered (Bayer) dithering for light falloff, fog and sky only
techniques.what: Use Bayer 4x4 or 8x8 thresholding between adjacent palette tones in gradients: headlamp falloff into darkness, depth fog, aurora curtains, snow haze. Mask it OFF on blocks and the hero.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It gives the moody dark-cave, cold-night feel with only a few colors, a signature retro look. Masking keeps block colors flat and readable. Indexing by snapped world texel keeps the pattern from shimmering while scrolling.
techniques.threejs_how: In the composite shader: ivec2 p = ivec2(gl_FragCoord.xy) + ivec2(camSnapOffsetTexels), threshold = bayer4[p % 4]. Pick the lower or upper of the two nearest palette entries in the LUT by luminance + threshold. Use the ID/mask channel from the outline MRT to skip blocks and hero. three.js also ships a TSL Bayer helper (module-Bayer) if we move to WebGPU/TSL. Blue noise (a 64^2 texture) is an option for a softer look.

techniques.name: Stepped pixel lighting: banded headlamp + darkness mask
techniques.what: Quantize all lighting into 2-4 hard bands. The hero's warm headlamp becomes a stepped radial pool (bright core, mid ring, dithered edge, darkness) that shrinks as depth increases or air runs low. Aurora and capsules get stepped glow.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This turns depth progression (500m going darker) into a strong mood and tension device, and keeps lighting consistent with pixel art. Smooth point-light gradients at low resolution look like banding errors, while deliberate bands look authored. The headlamp radius can also signal the air meter diegetically.
techniques.threejs_how: Swap MeshToonMaterial's gradientMap for a 3-texel NearestFilter ramp (already in place). For the headlamp, use a custom light term in onBeforeCompile: float d = length(worldPos.xy - heroPos.xy); band = floor(saturate(1 - d / R) * 3.0) / 3.0. Or do it as a screen-space darkness pass in the composite (cheaper on mobile: one uniform, no extra lights), multiplied before LUT and dither. Drop real-time shadow maps in pixel mode; use a stepped contact shadow blob under the hero and falling blocks (falling-block shadow is also a gameplay warning).

techniques.name: HD-2D-lite post stack at low res (bloom on emissives, layered depth haze)
techniques.what: Add a small bloom only on emissive pixels (aurora, stars, air capsules, lamp), a vertical tilt-shift blur on distant background layers (surface sky, far cave walls), and a light vignette. Composite these AFTER pixelation at screen res, or keep them pixelated for strict pixel mode.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It gives the 'premium diorama' polish of Octopath on top of pixel art and makes capsules pop as pickups. Bloom confined to emissives preserves block readability.
techniques.threejs_how: Mark emissives through the ID/mask channel. Downsample the low-res target 2x, threshold on the mask, do 2-3 separable blur taps, then add. That is cheap because the source is only about 270x480. Tilt-shift = blur applied only to background-layer meshes rendered into a separate low-res target (layers.set), not a depth-based DoF. Avoid UnrealBloomPass at full resolution on mobile.
