exemplar_games.what_to_steal: The full stable-pixel recipe: low internal res, snapped camera plus screen-space error offset, 1px depth/normal outlines with lighter crease highlights, toon lighting, and a sharp upscale filter. This is the technical gold standard for 'no shimmer'.

Flat cohesive shading, no AA, soft outlines for readability, and a player-facing pixel-size option. We could expose 'pixel size' in settings for mobile vs desktop and as a fallback for players who prefer crisp.
A 3D model rendered tiny without smoothing into pixel sprite frames, plus per-frame normal maps for in-game toon lighting. This is the exact route to animate the Yorkie hero with Tripo and Blender.
Billboarded pixel characters that cast real shadows inside a lit 3D diorama, with selective bloom, fog and tilt-shift. A template for our 'pixel hero in a 3D ice shaft with rich lighting' option.

Disciplined dithering: an 8x8 Bayer for smooth ramps vs blue noise for organic areas, and keeping dither dots 1:1 with output pixels to avoid shimmer. Apply it to cave darkness and aurora, not to blocks.

Eastward: '3D lighting + retro-pixel artwork', with real colored dynamic lights over hand-pixeled surfaces for warm/cold contrast (lamp amber vs ice blue). Dome Keeper (Godot): the closest genre match (digging down in pixel art). Steal the darkness-around-the-miner mood. Note: I found no Dome Keeper technical devlog, so its specifics are inferred from footage.

style_direction_ideas: A. 'Frozen Diorama Pixel' (t3ssel8r-faithful): ortho camera tilted about 8 degrees so block tops show a 2-3px frosty lip. 1 block = 16px, internal about 180x320 portrait. Color-ID 1px outlines around chunks with lighter crease pixels on top edges. 3-band toon, a 32-color palette with 4 reserved block hues, snap-then-offset smooth scrolling, and the Yorkie as a 24px Dead Cells-style normal-mapped sprite. Strongest 'feel' and most cohesive. Medium effort.

B. 'Midnight Driller 16-bit' (near-2D, mood-first): fully frontal ortho, so blocks read as SNES-like tiles that are still 3D for wobble/fall lighting. A strict about 20-color palette. The surface sky is a dithered aurora gradient with twinkling 1px stars. Below ground, darkness is a Bayer-dithered mask around the hero's stepped headlamp that shrinks with depth and low air (Dome Keeper vibe). Cheapest, safest on low-end mobile, and the most readable.

C. 'HD-2D Ice Cave' (pixel hero + pixel-textured blocks, rich modern light): blocks keep 16px nearest-filtered frost textures and pixel outlines in the low-res pass. Lighting, bloom on aurora/capsules, falling snow particles and depth haze are composited at higher resolution on top, Octopath-style. Most 'premium' looking and closest to Tidebreaker's moody-lit cohesion, but less pure pixel and medium mobile cost.

D. 'Hybrid toggle' (production hedge): build A's pipeline with pixel size as a uniform (1 = crisp flat-cartoon toon render, N = pixel art), with the palette LUT and dither as switches. The user likes both flat cartoon and pixel art, so this lets them A/B the same scene live before committing. The hero needs two sprite sets (cartoon at high res, pixel at the world's density).

research.angle: Readable stylized puzzle/arcade block games and dig games (Mr. Driller DrillLand, Puyo Puyo, Tetris Effect, Lumines, Meteos, SteamWorld Dig, Spelunky 2, Celeste, A Short Hike, Dome Keeper): how they keep block color/shape, falling hazards and the hero readable while still feeling atmospheric. Applied to an ICE WORLD Mr. Driller clone in Three.js that has to run on mobile.
key_insights: Readability comes from VALUE first, hue second. Celeste tilesets use only 3 indexed colors per tileset (light/mid/dark) plus 1 background color. Light colors go on edges as highlights. Every tileset shares the same dark 'infill' color, so playable solids separate from the background (sourced: aran.ink/posts/celeste-tilesets). Our counterpart: every block color needs a bright rim and a mid body. The cave background must sit in a value band the blocks never enter. (inferred application)

Never let color carry meaning alone. Puyo Puyo gives each color its own shape and eyes: yellow has a point on top, blue a tail, green is a perfect circle, purple a slanted oval. Later games add an Alphabet skin and colorblind palette menus (sourced: puyonexus wiki via search; gamedeveloper.com Saturn colorblind article). Color Universal Design (Okabe-Ito) recommends redundant coding with shape or pattern (sourced). With 4 colors per level we can give each color a fixed glyph or face. That serves accessibility and also gives the cute flat-cartoon charm the user likes. (inferred)

Lumines uses only 2 block colors per skin. Commentary notes that on crowded screens players 'start to only register visual contrasts', and that some skins with low-contrast block colors are hard to read (sourced: Lumines search results/PopMatters). Lesson: any beautiful skin has to pass a grayscale check. Our 4 colors need 4 clearly different luminance levels, or strong glyphs. (inferred)

Atmosphere belongs in the background and in light, not on the blocks. Spelunky 2 moved to heavier outlines and less distracting backgrounds. Players said that a background too detailed for the small foreground 'drowns out' sprites (sourced: forum summaries in search, mixed reliability). SteamWorld Dig uses a lamp radius plus darkness as both mood and mechanic, and block outlines stay visible even in darkness (sourced: pushsquare/pocketgamer reviews via search).

Low resolution can make a 3D world feel lush and readable if shading is flat and objects get a soft outline. A Short Hike: 'flat cohesive shading and no anti-aliasing' plus 'a soft outline effect to objects to help them stand out, and stay readable with so few pixels', and a player-adjustable pixel size (sourced: PlayStation Blog interview). This directly supports our existing pixel mode, which needs flat shading and outlines to work.

The falling-block threat must be telegraphed. In Mr. Driller, unsupported blocks shake for about a second before falling (sourced: obsoletegamer/HonestGamers via search). The shake is the main readability cue. It should be amplified with light and VFX, not just position jitter. (inferred)

Tetris Effect built most of its graphics from particles because particles react well to music. It alternates excitation and relaxation to help flow (sourced: Unreal Engine interview, via search summary; the page itself returned 403). For us, the 'gorgeous' moments should be pops and chains: ice shards and aurora flares. Idle blocks stay calm.

Meteos gives each planet its own block style, music and gravity (sourced: Wikipedia/fan wiki via search). A per-100m-level 'skin' (surface snow, then blue ice, then deep crystal, then black ice) gives progression without changing the gameplay palette logic. (inferred)

Real refraction is a mobile trap. MeshPhysicalMaterial transmission re-renders the scene for each transmissive material, and up to 2 extra passes with backside. Forum reports describe 100% GPU and broken rendering on some Android devices (sourced: three.js forum threads). Ice and gem looks should be faked inside a single-pass shader. (sourced + inferred)

Cohesion (the Tidebreaker feeling the user wants) comes from one restricted palette and one light story shared by hero, blocks and background. Dome Keeper's jam version used an 8-color palette at 320x270 (sourced: joshanthony.info design dive via search). Our hero billboard probably looks pasted-on because its palette and light don't match the 3D world. (inferred)

techniques.name: Value-banded 4-color palette + per-color glyph/face (redundant coding)
techniques.what: Choose the 4 block colors per level so their luminance differs clearly in grayscale, for example a pale cyan/white, a mid yellow-gold, a mid magenta and a dark-ish teal. Do not rely on red vs green. Give every color a fixed glyph, carved symbol or Puyo-style face (snowflake, star, heart, drop) that stays the same in every skin. Offer a colorblind palette swap.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Gameplay is about reading same-color chunks quickly while blocks move. A grayscale-safe palette plus shapes makes chunks readable for colorblind players and on dim phone screens. Faces/glyphs also add the flat-cartoon personality that matches the puppy hero.
techniques.threejs_how: Add a per-instance attribute colorIndex (InstancedBufferAttribute) to the instanced block mesh. In onBeforeCompile of MeshToonMaterial, or in a small custom ShaderMaterial, look up base/rim/shadow colors from a uniform vec3 palette[4*3]. Sample a 2x2 or 4x1 glyph atlas (generated with ChatGPT image, cleaned up into a single-channel mask) on the front face only, using the face normal. For merged chunks, draw the glyph once per chunk (on its centroid or largest cell) or on every cell at low opacity. A palette swap is just a uniform update. Validation: render a debug view with a grayscale post (luma) and check that the 4 colors separate.

references.title: Adapting Sega Saturn games to be colorblind-friendly (Puyo personality: eyes+shape; player palettes)
Puyo Nexus - List of Puyo skins (Alphabet skin etc.)
Coloring for Colorblindness (palette checker)
Lumines (two colors per skin; contrast issues in some skins)

techniques.name: Celeste-style chunk autotiling: shared dark infill, lit perimeter edges, one outline per chunk
techniques.what: Treat each same-color chunk as one blob rather than a cluster of outlined cubes. Exposed edges of the chunk get a bright highlight/bevel on the top-left light side and a darker lip on the bottom. Interior seams vanish. The outline is drawn only on the chunk perimeter. Optionally randomize 2-4 edge variants (icicles, snow caps on top edges) to break up the grid, as Celeste does with random edge-tile variants.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Chunk shape is the core gameplay information (what pops, what falls together). One clean silhouette per chunk reads much faster than many small outlined cubes, and it looks more designed. Snow caps on upward-facing edges sell the ICE WORLD for free.
techniques.threejs_how: Compute an 8-neighbor same-color mask per cell on the CPU when the grid changes and upload it as an instanced attribute (uint/float). In the fragment shader, use the mask plus the local face UV to decide whether a pixel lies near an exposed edge. If it does, add rim color and bevel shading, and push to black within N px for the outline. If not, use the flat body color. This replaces the inverted-hull outline for blocks: no second draw, and no hull artifacts between merged neighbors. For rounded-corner jelly/candy chunks, round only the convex corners via the mask (SDF of a rounded box per cell, clipped by the neighbor bits). Snow caps can be a second instanced mesh, spawned only where the up-neighbor is empty.

references.title: Celeste Tilesets, Step-by-Step (3 colors + infill, edge highlights, random edge variants)
BostonFIG talk: Celeste-style tilesets

techniques.name: Foreground/background value separation + depth darkness with headlamp (SteamWorld Dig model)
techniques.what: Lock the background (cave walls behind the shaft, sky, aurora) into a low-contrast, desaturated, darker value band. Blocks always sit above a minimum brightness and saturation. As depth increases, ambient light drops and the world goes navy and then near-black, but the hero's headlamp and a floor of self-illumination on blocks keep the play area readable. Falling blocks out of lamp range still keep their outline and glyph.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This gives the 'deeper and darker' mood the user wants without losing block-color reading, which is what SteamWorld Dig does. It also stops the aurora/sky from competing with blocks near the surface.
techniques.threejs_how: Render the background on its own layer/scene with its own fog, or bake it as cheap unlit planes with a ColorGrade uniform. For blocks, use a custom toon ramp where the final color is max(litColor, baseColor * minLumaFloor). The floor comes from a uniform tied to depth meters. Fake the headlamp in the block shader as a radial falloff from the hero's screen/world position: one uniform vec3, no real PointLight shadow cost. Keep the single directional light for the hero/contact shadow. Fog: THREE.Fog only on background materials (fog:false on blocks) so blocks never wash out.

references.title: SteamWorld Dig review (light meter shrinks view distance; outlines remain in darkness)
Spelunky 2 discussion (heavier outlines, less distracting backgrounds)
Dome Keeper design dive (depth darkness, lamp, lit edges)

techniques.name: Fake 'ice-candy / gem' interior: interior mapping + fresnel rim + matcap, NOT transmission
techniques.what: Make blocks look like translucent ice or jelly candy with a glowing core: a darker refracted inner cube or bubbles that parallax as the camera moves, a bright fresnel rim, and a sharp specular matcap highlight. All of it is single-pass and opaque.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is the 'gorgeous' factor for an ice world. Parallax interiors feel deep and premium, and an opaque shader keeps the same draw cost as now. Because the core is the saturated block color and the rim is bright, it reinforces the value-band rule rather than fighting it.
techniques.threejs_how: Custom ShaderMaterial (or onBeforeCompile on MeshMatcapMaterial) on the instanced cube. (1) Interior mapping: transform the view dir into the cube's local space and intersect with an inner box scaled about 0.7. Shade the hit by depth, which gives a darker core plus a lighter shell. Optionally sample a small 64px cubemap/2D noise for bubbles/cracks. That is about 4 lines of math plus 1 texture read. (2) Fresnel rim: pow(1-dot(N,V),3) * rimColor. (3) Matcap texture painted to match the flat-cartoon highlight shape (one hard white blob). Avoid MeshPhysicalMaterial.transmission: each transmissive material re-renders the scene. Blender headless can bake the matcap from a sphere with the target toon material.

references.title: My take on shaders: Interior mapping (ray-box in tangent space + cubemap)
Faking refraction in three.js
three.js forum: transmission performance (extra full-scene passes)
three.js forum: transmission broken on some Android devices

techniques.name: Falling-hazard telegraph stack: shake + light pulse + crack + drop shadow on the hero column
techniques.what: Mr. Driller's core warning is that unsupported blocks shake for about a second before they fall. Layer more cues on top of the jitter: an emissive white/red pulse that speeds up, frost-crack decals, a small ice-dust particle drip, and a projected 'danger shadow' strip on whatever is below, including the hero.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Getting crushed is the main way to die, so the threat must read even in pixel mode and in dark depths where color is harder to see. Light pulses and shadows read in peripheral vision better than small position jitter.
techniques.threejs_how: Per-instance attributes wobbleT (0-1) and fallState. The vertex shader does a sine jitter whose amplitude follows a curve over wobbleT. The fragment shader adds emissive = pulse(wobbleT) * warnColor, and a crack mask from a tiny atlas when wobbleT > 0.5. Danger shadow: one instanced quad per falling chunk column, drawn on the face below with multiply blending and its opacity tied to time-to-impact. Dust: a pooled THREE.Points with a custom point shader. All of this is cheap.

references.title: Mr. Driller (blocks shake ~1 second before falling)
HonestGamers Mr. Driller review (blocks quiver before descent)

techniques.name: A Short Hike-style low-res pipeline: fixed vertical resolution, integer upscale, flat shading, no AA, soft outline
techniques.what: Render the 3D scene at a fixed low internal height (for example about 270-360 lines), with no MSAA, flat or 2-3 step toon shading, and an outline. Then nearest-neighbor upscale by an integer factor. Let the player pick the pixel size. Snap the camera to the pixel grid to avoid shimmering.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The user likes pixel art. Low-res unifies the hero sprite, 3D blocks and VFX into one look, which is the cohesion that Tidebreaker has and ours lacks. It also cuts fill-rate cost on mobile.
techniques.threejs_how: renderer.setPixelRatio(1) plus a WebGLRenderTarget at (internalH * aspect, internalH) with NearestFilter, then a fullscreen quad blit (or the existing CSS image-rendering: pixelated, which works if the canvas size is an integer multiple). Snap the camera's world position to the texel size (worldUnitsPerPixel) each frame. The three/examples RenderPixelatedPass (addons/postprocessing/RenderPixelatedPass.js) also provides depth/normal-edge outlines in one pass. Draw the hero sprite at the same pixel density as the internal render (author it at the target pixel height) so pixels match.

references.title: PlayStation Blog: Crafting a tiny open world (A Short Hike) - flat shading, no AA, soft outline, adjustable pixel size
three.js RenderPixelatedPass example

techniques.name: Restricted palette / depth-driven color grade (LUT or palette quantize final pass)
techniques.what: Push the whole frame (hero, blocks, background, VFX) through one shared palette or LUT, ideally 16-32 colors, in the spirit of Celeste's 3-5 colors per tileset and Dome Keeper's 8-color jam palette. Crossfade LUTs by depth: surface night (indigo + aurora green), blue ice, deep crystal (violet/cyan), abyss (near-black blue), while block hues stay locked.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is the fastest way to make the AI-made hero sprite, Tripo props and procedural blocks feel like one game. It also gives each 100m level its own mood (Meteos-like per-planet identity) without retuning materials.
techniques.threejs_how: Single fullscreen pass after the scene render (or merged into the upscale blit). Use LUTPass from three/examples (addons/postprocessing/LUTPass.js) with 2 small 3D LUTs and a uniform mix by depth, or a custom nearest-color palette quantize for pixel mode with optional ordered Bayer dithering. Exclude block cores from grading by writing them pre-graded, or keep the LUT neutral on the 4 gameplay hues. Cost is one texture fetch per pixel at low internal res.

references.title: Celeste Tilesets, Step-by-Step (limited per-tileset colors)
Design Dive: Dome Keeper (8-color palette, 320x270)
Meteos (each planet own block style/music/gravity)
three.js LUT example

techniques.name: Threshold-gated emissive bloom only on 'meaningful light'
techniques.what: Bloom applies only to what matters or what should feel magical: air capsules, pop flashes, chain counters, aurora and the hero headlamp. Idle blocks never bloom, so chunk edges stay crisp.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Glow is the cheapest 'wow' for a night/ice theme. Gating it means it never blurs the gameplay grid. Air capsules glowing at depth become a strong navigation cue.
techniques.threejs_how: Set the bloom threshold to 1.0 or higher and give only the chosen materials emissiveIntensity > 1 (HDR via HalfFloat render target), so no layer juggling is needed. Use UnrealBloomPass (three/examples) at half or quarter resolution, or pmndrs/postprocessing BloomEffect with mipmapBlur, which is cheaper. Turn it off on low-tier devices via a quality toggle. In pixel mode, run bloom at the low internal res so the glow also pixelates.

references.title: three.js example: bloom emissive (webgpu)
Unreal Bloom selective - Wael Yasmina
pmndrs postprocessing selective bloom discussion

techniques.name: Particle-first juice for pops/chains (Tetris Effect principle), calm idle state
techniques.what: When a chunk pops, it shatters into ice shards and snow puffs in the block's color, and a flash sweeps along the chunk outline. Chains escalate: more shards, a short aurora flare across the background, a small camera kick. Idle blocks stay calm and still, which creates an excitation/relaxation rhythm.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is where the 'feel' lives. Celebratory moments get spectacle while the readable grid stays clean the rest of the time. Shards in the block's color also confirm which color popped.
techniques.threejs_how: A pooled InstancedMesh of tiny tetrahedra/quads (about 500 max) with per-instance velocity and life in attributes, simulated in the vertex shader from spawn time (no CPU per-frame update). A THREE.Points snow puff with additive blending. Aurora flare: drive a uniform on the existing aurora shader. Screen shake: camera offset, snapped to the pixel grid in pixel mode. Hit-stop: freeze gameplay for 2-4 frames on large pops.

references.title: Unreal Engine: How Tetris Effect became a modern work of art (particles as base; excitation/relaxation cycle)

techniques.name: Hero readability: own rim light + outline + matching pixel density and palette
techniques.what: The hero must never be lost against same-value blocks. Give the sprite a 1-2 px dark outline, a cool rim/backlight from the 'aurora side', and a headlamp glow that defines its column. Author it at the same pixel density and palette as the world. Even 2-3 frame dig and squash animations matter more than detail.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The user perceives the current billboard as awkward. A mismatch in pixel density, lighting and palette is the usual cause of the 'pasted-on sprite' look, and Celeste and A Short Hike both lean on outlines to separate characters.
techniques.threejs_how: Keep the billboard, but light it with a custom sprite shader: albedo * (ambient band from the depth uniform) + rim (alpha-gradient edge detection via 4 offset alpha samples, which also produces the outline in the same shader) + lamp. Use alphaTest for crisp pixels. In pixel mode, render the sprite at the internal res with NearestFilter and snap its position to texels. For animation frames, use a flipbook UV offset uniform on a sprite atlas.

references.title: My Thoughts on Very Low Resolution (outlines separate sprites from background)
A Short Hike soft outline for readability

exemplar_games.what_to_steal: Each color has its own body shape and facial expression. Same-color pieces visually fuse into blobs. Colorblind skins and palettes. This is the model for cute, readable, mergeable blocks that match a flat-cartoon puppy.

3-color tilesets plus one shared dark infill. Light edge highlights separate solids from the background. Random edge variants break up the grid. Snow as white blobs on blue-gray. Use this as the rule set for chunk perimeter rendering.
Low-res 3D with flat shading, no AA and soft outlines, plus an adjustable pixel size. This is a direct template for our pixel mode and for unifying the 2D hero with the 3D world in a snowy setting.
Lamp-radius lighting as mood and tension, with block outlines that stay readable in darkness. Layered backdrops behind a clean dig grid. This is how 'deeper = darker' can work without hurting play.

Per-stage skins tied to music and mood. Particle-driven spectacle on clears. Also a warning: skins where block colors lack contrast against the background become hard to read. Check every skin in grayscale.

The original's bold, saturated, glossy blocks and the 1-second pre-fall shake. Angular, flat, early-2000s cartoon character style (reviews compare it to Dexter's Lab). Each attraction gets its own visual theme while the core block language stays the same.

style_direction_ideas: A) 'FROST CANDY' (flat cartoon, recommended for charm): blocks are glossy ice-jelly blobs with rounded convex corners, a carved snowflake/star/heart/drop glyph or a tiny Puyo-like face per color, a hard white matcap highlight, a bright rim and bold black outlines only on the chunk perimeter. Snow caps sit on top edges. The background is a soft-painted, low-contrast night (indigo plus a muted green aurora). The hero uses the flat cartoon sprite with the same outline weight. Techniques: glyph palette, chunk autotile, interior mapping off or subtle, threshold bloom on capsules and pops only.

B) 'AURORA PIXEL' (A Short Hike meets Celeste, recommended for cohesion): the same 3D scene rendered at about 300 lines, integer-scaled, with a 24-32 color master palette and LUTs crossfaded by depth. Toon shading is flat, 2 steps. A soft outline comes from RenderPixelatedPass. The pixel-art hero sprite is authored at matching density. Blocks use Celeste-style 3-tone edges plus a 5x5 px glyph. The aurora and stars use ordered dithering. This is the cheapest to run on mobile and the most unified look.

C) 'CRYSTAL DEEP' (moody, Tidebreaker-like atmosphere): the surface is snowy night. With depth, the shaft turns into a dark crystal cave lit mainly by the puppy's warm headlamp and by blocks that glow from inside (interior-mapped cores and fresnel rims). X-blocks are matte, frosted, brown-gray stone with no glow, so they read as 'different material'. Air capsules bloom. The palette goes warm hero light against cool world, the same lamp-vs-night contrast Tidebreaker uses. Watch the value floor so blocks never sink into the dark.

D) 'LEVEL SKINS' hybrid (Meteos/Lumines approach): keep the gameplay layer fixed (glyphs, palette value bands, chunk outlines, hazard telegraph) and switch an environment and material skin every 100m: 0-100 snowfield (Frost Candy), 100-200 blue glacier (clear ice with bubbles), 200-300 aurora caverns (emissive rims), 300-400 crystal geode (faceted gems), 400-500 black ice abyss (headlamp only). Progression feels like a journey, and each skin is a uniform/LUT/material swap on the same shader.

research.angle: Mood, lighting and juice for a night ice cave that gets darker with depth. The aim is atmosphere a phone browser can afford in Three.js, without hurting how quickly the player reads block colours, chunk shapes and falling blocks.
key_insights: Fog and contrast do most of the work in atmospheric games, not expensive light simulation. Playdead said many early INSIDE scenes were essentially fog plus silhouettes [sourced: Playdead GDC 2016 rendering talk summary]. Ori used a custom fog whose colour and transparency blend in over depth [sourced: Ori artdump on polycount, via search summary]. Hollow Knight lit its scenes with soft transparent shapes and makes the player the brightest light in its darker areas [sourced: medium.com 'The Art of Hollow Knight', via search summary]. For us this means fog colour per depth band, a few additive light blobs and a strong figure-ground split, before any real-time GI or volumetric work [inferred].

Keep a strict layer hierarchy. Hollow Knight gives the playable middle ground stronger contrast and thicker outlines than the foreground and background [sourced]. Ori keeps the hero a near-white silhouette against busy painted backgrounds [sourced: GDC 2015 Ori animation notes]. In our game the coloured blocks must always be the most saturated, highest-contrast thing on screen. Fog, aurora and grading should act mostly on the background, sky and empty space, not on block hues [inferred].

A probable cause of our 'awkward' look: the hero billboard is lit by the scene lights while the toon cubes use a 3-step ramp. That gives two different lighting languages. Ori lit its character as 100% self-illuminated and faked direction with an additive/multiply mask on one side, which stays correct when the sprite flips [sourced]. A 2D hero that is self-lit plus a rim from the dominant light (warm headlamp or cool aurora) will sit in the 3D world better than a naively lit quad [inferred].

Tidebreaker looks cohesive because it is low-key and has one dominant contrast: a dark sea against warm lamp light. Its own description is 'A dark sea. A waking giant. A lighthouse to reach.' [sourced: tidebreaker.vercel.app]. The author's pipeline was GPT Images for mockups, Blender + Tripo for 3D and Spriterrific for 2D sprites [sourced: chongdashu on X]. The lesson to take is one warm key light in a cold world with most of the frame in shadow, not the tools themselves [inferred].

Restraint is a technique in its own right. Playdead gave a VFX talk titled 'Turn it Down 90%' about clean shapes and muted colours [sourced: Playdead publications page]. They also used two separate glow passes, a wide fog-glow and a narrow glow, because the two interfered when combined. They used dithering against colour banding [sourced]. Dark gradient-heavy scenes like an ice cave band badly on 8-bit mobile output, so a blue-noise dither in the final pass is cheap insurance [inferred].

Darkness with depth can be a gameplay system as well as a mood. A screen-space lightmap (additive blobs, then multiplied over the scene) is the standard cheap 2D approach [sourced: slembcke.net 2D Lighting Techniques]. If the headlamp radius and ambient floor shrink with depth, difficulty and atmosphere rise together. Block hues must stay identifiable at the ambient floor, for example with a minimum ambient level plus emissive colour edges, or the 4-pop logic becomes unfair [inferred].

Juice should be scaled to the size of the event and should be optional. Eiserloh's trauma model keeps a 0-1 value, adds to it on hits, decays it linearly, and shakes by trauma squared or cubed [sourced: GDC 2016 'Juicing Your Cameras With Math']. Nijman's 'Art of Screenshake' covers hit-stop and camera kick [sourced]. Celeste ships a screen-shake option with 50% as the default [sourced: Steam discussion via search]. We should add a shake/flash setting and keep shake off the parts of the frame where the player reads falling blocks [inferred].

In Three.js, merge the post stack into as few full-screen passes as possible. pmndrs/postprocessing merges multiple effects in one EffectPass into a single compound shader. Effects that change screen coordinates, such as chromatic aberration, may need their own pass [sourced: pmndrs wiki 'Effect Merging']. On mobile the cost is mostly passes times resolution, so a budget of scene + half-res lightmap + mip bloom + one merged composite pass is realistic. Our existing pixel mode (low-res render target) helps a great deal here [inferred].

techniques.name: Fake translucent ice blocks (thickness-based backlight + fresnel rim + inner glow)
techniques.what: Use the Barré-Brisebois/Bouchard GDC 2011 cheap translucency approximation: H = normalize(L + N*distortion); I = attenuation * (pow(saturate(dot(V,-H)), power)*scale + ambient) * thickness [sourced: Alan Zucconi's write-up of the talk]. Thickness comes from a local thickness map, which can be baked by flipping the mesh faces, rendering AO, and inverting it [sourced]. Add a fresnel rim and a faint emissive 'core' so blocks read as glassy ice rather than painted cubes.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: This is the single biggest jump from 'toon cubes' to 'ice world'. When the hero's headlamp sits behind or beside a block, the ice glows through in its own colour, which reinforces chunk colour instead of washing it out. It also gives a natural place to signal state: frozen X-blocks are opaque with no translucency, and wobbling blocks pulse their glow [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Extend the existing MeshToonMaterial with onBeforeCompile, or use a small custom ShaderMaterial that works with InstancedMesh. Pass the headlamp position as a uniform and compute the translucency term against it only, not all lights. Thickness can be a per-instance attribute: 1 at chunk edges and less in the middle of merged chunks, so chunk silhouettes glow. Alternatively use a tiny baked texture for the cube, since a Blender headless bake of inverted-normal AO is trivial for a cube or bevelled cube. Fresnel is pow(1 - dot(N,V), k) times the block colour, added to emissive. Keep the toon ramp for diffuse and add translucency after the ramp so the flat cartoon look survives [inferred].

Barré-Brisebois GDC 2011 - Approximating Translucency for a Fast, Cheap and Convincing SSS Look
Approximating Translucency Revisited

techniques.name: Headlamp darkness-reveal lightmap (screen-space 2D light buffer)
techniques.what: Each frame, draw soft additive light blobs into a small offscreen buffer: a headlamp cone or circle around the hero, glows on air capsules, a bright flash at popping chains, and a cool aurora band near the surface. Multiply that buffer over the scene. This is the classic screen-space lightmap: blobs drawn with the same camera, then multiplied over the framebuffer [sourced: slembcke.net].
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It turns 'gets darker with depth' into a readable mechanic. The ambient floor and headlamp radius shrink per 100m band, capsules become beacons, and chains light the cave for a moment, which is a reward that also feels good. It is much cheaper and more controllable than many real Three.js PointLights, and it gives the Hollow Knight 'player is the brightest light' feel [inferred]. For readability, never multiply below an ambient floor, roughly enough to tell 4 hues apart. Keep a thin emissive colour edge on blocks so shapes read in the dark [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use a WebGLRenderTarget at 1/4 to 1/2 resolution and a separate Scene of THREE.Sprite or instanced quads with a radial-gradient texture and AdditiveBlending, rendered with the main camera. Composite in the final pass as color *= max(ambientFloor, lightmap). Use one real three.js PointLight for the headlamp so the toon shading and translucency still respond. The lightmap handles everything else. In pixel mode the lightmap can be very low resolution [inferred].

references.title: slembcke - 2D Lighting Techniques
The Art of Hollow Knight (lighting with soft transparent shapes; player as brightest light)

techniques.name: Per-depth-band colour grading (LUT or parametric) with environment-first grading
techniques.what: Each 100m level gets its own grade. For example: surface is aurora teal/violet with warm lamp; 100-200m is cold cyan ice; 200-300m is deep blue; 300-400m is indigo/near-black with warm headlamp; 400-500m is a goal zone with a new accent such as glowing geode amber. Crossfade between grades as the camera descends. This follows Gris, where each stage introduces one new colour to the palette [sourced: Gris interviews/articles via search].
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It gives a sense of progress and a distinct identity per 100m level for almost no cost, and it makes the 500m goal feel like a journey [inferred]. Risk: a full-screen LUT also shifts block hues and can make two of the four block colours look alike in a band. Grade the environment more strongly than the blocks [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Option A, cheapest and safest for readability: drive scene uniforms per band, namely fog colour and density, hemisphere sky and ground colours, background wall tint and lightmap ambient. Blocks keep their palette and receive only a light shared tint. Option B: three/addons LUTPass, or pmndrs LUT3DEffect inside the merged EffectPass, with two LUTs blended by a uniform. LUTs can be authored as .cube files in any photo tool [sourced: three.js LUTPass docs, PR #20558]. Interpolate on camera depth, not discretely, so there are no pops [inferred].

Gris - Wikipedia (colour-per-stage progression)

techniques.name: Layered depth fog + parallax cave walls + gradient sky + fake light shafts
techniques.what: Build depth from 2-4 background planes (far ice wall, mid icicles and stalactites, near foreground frost framing the shaft edges) that scroll at different rates. Fog the back layers more with fog colour that changes over depth, as Ori did with its custom depth fog [sourced: Ori artdump summary] and Hollow Knight with stacked parallax and fog layers [sourced]. The sky is a vertex-colour gradient quad, the trick Alto's Adventure used to keep draw calls minimal [sourced: Alto search summary of Harry Nesbitt's making-of]. Light shafts from the surface opening are additive gradient cone meshes with scrolling noise.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Our 9-column shaft is visually flat. Parallax layers outside the playfield make it feel like a vast frozen cave while the playfield stays clean. The near-foreground frost vignette also frames the playable columns [inferred]. Fake shaft meshes give the INSIDE and Ori volumetric feel at the surface for nearly zero cost [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use simple PlaneGeometry layers with MeshBasicMaterial and transparent textures from ChatGPT image, tinted by a per-band uniform. Use built-in scene.fog (THREE.Fog) for the 3D walls, or put the fog in the layer shader as mix(color, fogColor, layerDepth). Parallax is camera.y times a factor per layer. Light shafts are a few cone or quad meshes with additive blending, depthWrite off, a vertical-falloff gradient and a uv-scrolled noise texture, faded out below about 50m. Avoid raymarched screen-space god rays on mobile: three-good-godrays is a raymarched pmndrs pass and much heavier [inferred from its description].

The Art of Hollow Knight (three layers, parallax, fog)

techniques.name: Selective mip bloom (two kinds of glow) + blue-noise dither
techniques.what: Bloom only what should glow: air capsules, chain-pop flashes, aurora, translucent rims and maybe the headlamp source. INSIDE used two separate glow passes, a wide fog-glow and a narrow glow, because the two interfered when combined. It also used dithering to fight banding [sourced: Playdead GDC 2016]. A 'wide' glow can be faked by the lightmap from the previous technique, so the post bloom can stay narrow and cheap [inferred].
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Capsules must pop out as a survival resource, and chains need a payoff flash. Bloom on HDR emissive only does both without blurring block edges. Dark blue gradients band on phones, and dithering removes that 'cheap web game' tell [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use pmndrs BloomEffect with mipmapBlur, a high luminanceThreshold, and emissive values above 1.0 only on glow objects, which avoids a separate layer render. Use fewer mip levels on low-tier devices [sourced: playbooks/postfx summary of mipmapBlur and levels]. Alternatively use three/addons UnrealBloomPass with the selective layer technique, which costs an extra scene render [sourced: Wael Yasmina tutorial]. Add an 8x8 or 64x64 blue-noise texture times 1/255 in the final merged pass [inferred].

techniques.name: Cheap 2D aurora curtain + aurora light spill
techniques.what: Draw an animated aurora above the surface as a 2D shader on a sky plane: stacked FBM-noise ribbons with vertical falloff and a teal-to-violet gradient, plus twinkling star points. Avoid the raymarched Shadertoy-style volumetric aurora. Spill its colour onto the surface snow and top blocks by animating the hemisphere-light sky colour and a top-of-screen lightmap band in sync with aurora brightness.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: The surface start is the first impression and the title-screen shot. A living aurora that tints the snow ties the sky to the play area, which is the cohesion the user feels is missing. As the hero digs, the aurora spill fades, and that fading is itself the 'going deeper' cue [inferred]. Raymarched aurora shaders are noted as performance-heavy, with quality tiers offering 8, 12 or 16 steps [sourced: aurora shader search results].
techniques.threejs_how: Use a ShaderMaterial on a large plane behind everything: 2-3 octaves of value noise scrolled in time, shaped into curtains with uv.x warping, alpha multiplied by smoothstep in uv.y, additive blend, rendered at lightmap resolution if needed. Stars are THREE.Points with a per-point twinkle phase. Spill is one uniform, auroraIntensity(t), feeding the hemisphere light colour and the lightmap top band [inferred].

techniques.name: Ori-style self-lit hero sprite with directional rim mask
techniques.what: Stop lighting the hero billboard with the scene lights. Render it as unlit (self-illuminated) and add a tinted rim or edge-light mask on the side facing the dominant light: cool aurora from above at the surface, warm headlamp spill or capsule glow deeper down. The mask stays correct when the sprite flips. This is how Ori faked lighting on a 100% self-illuminated character [sourced: GDC 2015 Ori animation notes].
techniques.why_it_helps_us: It fixes the mismatch between a 2D sprite and 3D toon blocks, and it keeps the Yorkie always readable, as the near-white silhouette principle did for Ori. It works the same for the flat-cartoon and pixel candidates [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use a ShaderMaterial on the hero plane. Sample the sprite and alpha-test it. Compute a cheap edge mask from alpha by sampling alpha at uv plus or minus an offset along the light direction and taking the difference. Add rimColor times mask. Optionally add a 1-2px outline from the same alpha samples so the hero matches the inverted-hull block outlines. Pass lightDir and rimColor uniforms from the active light context. Keep the existing contact shadow [inferred].

techniques.name: Juice kit: trauma shake, hit-stop, squash and stretch, telegraphed wobble
techniques.what: Use trauma-based camera shake: trauma 0-1, add on events, decay linearly, offset by trauma squared or cubed through smooth noise [sourced: Eiserloh GDC 2016]. Add hit-stop, a few frames of freeze on heavy impacts [sourced: Nijman 'Art of Screenshake']. Squash and stretch the hero and the blocks: Ori exaggerated hard, squashing to about '10 pixels' on landing [sourced]. Sizes: small hits shake little, chain pops get hit-stop plus a radial flash, crushes get the largest shake.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Digging and chain pops need a tactile payoff, and the wobble before a block falls is the key gameplay telegraph, so it should be the most deliberate animation in the game. Exaggerate the wobble with jitter, frost dust falling from the seam and a creak flash so falling danger reads from the corner of the eye [inferred]. A shake intensity setting follows Celeste's precedent, which ships 50% as the default [sourced].
techniques.threejs_how: Apply camera offset and roll from trauma via simplex noise in the render loop, never moving the logic grid. Implement hit-stop as a timeScale that goes to 0 for N ms on the simulation clock while particles and shaders keep running. Block squash goes through a per-instance scale attribute or matrix tweak on the InstancedMesh, using an easeOutElastic over about 150 ms after landing. Hero squash and stretch is already done in code; add anticipation before the dig and a landing squash [inferred].

techniques.name: Pooled GPU particles: snow, ice shards, frost dust, breath fog, glints
techniques.what: Particle effects: falling snow and drifting ice motes in 2 parallax layers; ice shards on each dig, tinted with the dug block's colour; frost dust trickling from blocks about to fall; little breath-fog puffs from the hero at intervals, bigger when air is low; sparkle glints on frost and capsules; and a confetti burst of shards plus a light flash on chain pops.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Particles sell 'cold' more than any texture does. Breath fog that grows as air runs low turns a HUD stat into a diegetic mood cue. Colour-tinted shards confirm which chunk was hit [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use one THREE.Points, or one InstancedMesh of camera-facing quads per effect family, with a ShaderMaterial. Spawn data goes into a ring buffer of attributes (birthTime, velocity, colour) and motion is computed in the vertex shader from time, so there are no per-frame CPU uploads beyond new spawns. Use small soft textures in a single atlas. Watch overdraw: big translucent breath puffs are the expensive ones on mobile, so keep them few and small. In pixel mode, particles render at low resolution for free [inferred].

techniques.name: One merged composite pass: vignette, event-only chromatic aberration, grain, dither, lightmap multiply
techniques.what: A single final full-screen shader does lightmap multiply, grade, a vignette whose strength grows with depth and as air drops, blue-noise dither and very light grain. Radial chromatic aberration is pulsed only on crush, low-air and chain events, never constant.
techniques.why_it_helps_us: Vignette focuses the eye on the hero column and strengthens the 'deeper = more enclosed' feeling. Constant chromatic aberration would smear block edges and hurt colour reading, so it is used only as a hit accent [inferred]. One pass keeps mobile cost flat [inferred].
techniques.threejs_how: Use pmndrs EffectPass with VignetteEffect, NoiseEffect, a custom lightmap-multiply effect, the LUT and bloom merged into one shader [sourced: pmndrs Effect Merging wiki]. Put ChromaticAberrationEffect in its own pass, or do the custom effect's uv offset in the same shader, enabled only when its intensity is above 0, because the wiki warns that effects which modify screen coordinates do not merge cleanly [sourced]. Alternatively, write one hand-rolled ShaderPass with three/addons EffectComposer [inferred].

exemplar_games.game: Ori and the Blind Forest (Moon Studios)
exemplar_games.what_to_steal: A self-illuminated hero with an additive/multiply light mask that keeps its direction when the sprite flips, which solves our sprite-vs-3D mismatch. Custom depth fog whose colour and transparency blend over depth. Exaggerated squash on landing. Hero silhouette that stays bright against busy backgrounds.

Fog plus silhouettes as the core of the mood. Two separate glow types (wide fog-glow and narrow glow). Dithering against banding in dark gradients. The 'Turn it Down 90%' restraint of muted colours and clean shapes. They also have an iOS shipping talk worth reading for mobile.

Three-layer composition with the gameplay layer at the highest contrast and with thicker outlines. Soft transparent shapes for lighting instead of real lights. Lighting that dims in ominous areas, where the player is the brightest light, which maps directly onto our headlamp at depth.

exemplar_games.game: Alto's Adventure / Odyssey (Team Alto, Harry Nesbitt)
exemplar_games.what_to_steal: Minimalist, impressionistic snow art. Vertex-colour gradient skies at near-zero draw cost. Atmospheric layering and weather as the main mood carriers. Our surface and aurora scene should feel like an Alto night level.

Palette progression as narrative: each stage introduces a new colour. This maps onto our five 100m depth bands, where each band gets its own grade and the final band can bring in one new accent colour as a reward for reaching 500m.

A 3D-to-pixel pipeline: tiny renders without antialiasing plus a basic toon shader. This validates our 'render 3D at low res, upscale pixelated' mode. It also suggests building hero animation frames from a rigged 3D model (Tripo + Blender) rendered at low resolution, if hand-drawn frames prove hard.

style_direction_ideas: A. 'Lantern in the Deep' (INSIDE / Hollow Knight / Tidebreaker). The environment is desaturated cold blue and fog-heavy, with mostly near-black parallax walls. The only saturated things are the coloured ice blocks and the warm amber headlamp. The darkness-reveal lightmap matters most here. Ambient shrinks per 100m, capsules and chain flashes are the only other light sources, bloom is minimal, and there is a strong vignette at depth. It is the most cohesive and moody direction and the closest to the Tidebreaker feel the user admired. Risk: deep levels can get too dark, so it needs an ambient floor and emissive block edges [inferred].

B. 'Aurora Candy' (Alto's Odyssey / Gris, flat cartoon). Pastel gradient skies, a vivid teal-violet aurora that spills onto snow, bold inverted-hull outlines on blocks and a matching sprite outline on the flat-cartoon hero. The cave gets darker but stays colourful through per-band grading (cyan, blue, indigo, violet, gold geode at the goal). Bloom is generous on capsules and chains, there are lots of snow and shard particles, and the juice is bouncy. It is the friendliest look, the most readable and the easiest to keep fast on mobile [inferred].

C. 'Frozen Pixel' (Dead Cells pipeline). Commit to the low-resolution pixel mode: render the 3D toon blocks at about 270-360 lines, upscale nearest-neighbour, use a 2-step toon ramp, dither gradients in the fog and lightmap instead of smooth falloff, and optionally quantise to a limited ice palette in the final pass. The pixel-art Yorkie fits naturally, and the hero's animation frames could come from a Tripo/Blender rig rendered at low resolution. It is the cheapest on GPU and the most stylistically forgiving of AI-asset inconsistencies [inferred].

D. 'Crystal Geode' (translucency-first). Make the fake-SSS ice the hero of the look. Blocks are glassy, gem-like and glow from within when the headlamp passes behind them. Deep down, blocks become dim light sources in their own colour, so the darkness itself reveals chunk shapes as glowing veins. Frozen X-blocks are opaque, dull and frost-crusted for contrast. Aurora at the top, a warm headlamp and jewel tones in the dark. It is the most distinctive, 'never seen this in a Mr. Driller clone' option, but it needs careful tuning so translucency never changes perceived block hue [inferred].

diagnosis: 1. Two lighting models, and the hero is lit twice. The blocks use a hard 3-step MeshToonMaterial ramp, while the hero is a MeshLambertMaterial plane with smooth falloff. On top of that, the AI sprite already has highlights and shadows painted in, so the scene lights it a second time from a direction that doesn't match. The eye reads this as two different renderers. This is the main cause of the 'sticker between boxes' look (src/main3d.ts around line 270).

2. Texel density and dimensionality don't match. A dense HD illustration (or a pixel sprite minified with linear filtering and mipmaps) sits next to flat-colored cubes with a procedural frost texture. The drill is a real 3D primitive attached to a flat card, so its parallax shows the puppy is paper (main3d.ts lines 255-318).

3. The ink rules don't match. Block outlines are inverted hulls in world units, so their screen width changes with depth and perspective. The sprite's ink is baked in at whatever weight the AI picked, then softened by downscaling. Matching line weight is the strongest cohesion cue in flat-cartoon and pixel styles.

4. The camera projection fights the art. A near-frontal perspective camera shows side faces on the outer columns and pulls the shaft toward a vanishing point, next to a strictly front-view sprite. In pixel mode, perspective also makes stable pixels impossible: pixel creep can only be solved under orthographic projection (Texel Splatting / ProPixelizer).

5. A single front-view pose slides sideways and digs down. With no turn, dig, anticipation or landing frames, it moves like a cut-out pushed across a board, however good the shading is. Tidebreaker holds together largely because it has a full idle/walk/run/jump/hurt set made from one reference.

6. The hero isn't sitting inside the space. The plane floats in front of the carved cell, and a contact shadow is the only cue. The cavity has no dark interior faces, no occlusion, no rim light and no overlap from the block lip above, so the puppy reads as 'on the glass' rather than 'in the hole'.

7. There is no shared palette or grade. AI sprite colors, toon-lit block colors and fog each live in their own color world, and ACES tone mapping desaturates and shifts flat brand colors. Nothing at the end of the pipeline forces them onto one palette.

8. There is no value hierarchy or atmosphere layering. Sky, playfield and hero compete at similar contrast. There are no background or foreground layers, so the hero is the only thing on screen that looks drawn and looks foreign. The 'one warm key in a cold world' story that makes Tidebreaker cohere is missing.
universal_fixes: Camera: switch to an OrthographicCamera, or a very narrow FOV (about 10-15 deg) pulled far back, with 0-8 deg tilt so block tops show a small frost lip. Required for pixel mode and good for every option.

One shading rule for everything on screen. Regenerate the hero sprite as flat albedo with no painted lighting (at most one shadow tone), then light it with the same function as the blocks (shared toon ramp or self-lit plus rim). Draw the drill into the sprite frames; never attach a 3D primitive to a 2D card.

One ink rule. Replace inverted hulls with a screen-space outline driven by chunk-ID and depth edges, at a constant pixel width. Merged same-color chunks then get one perimeter line and no inner seams. The hero writes its own ID to get the same line. This also removes the second instanced draw.

Texel-density lock: fix pixels per cell (for example 16/24 for pixel, 48 for cartoon) and author the sprite, block textures and particles to it. Sprite textures use NearestFilter with no mipmaps in pixel styles, and the hero is about 1.2-1.5 cells tall.

Grounding kit: sprite aligned to the camera plane and pivoted at the feet, alphaTest so it writes depth, a radial blob shadow that shrinks on hops, inset cavity wall meshes with darker ramp and vertex AO, and the front lip of the block above slightly overlapping the sprite.

A minimum animation set before any style polish: idle (2f), side walk (4f), dig-side (3f), dig-down (3f), fall, land-squash, crushed, out-of-air. Play as a UV flipbook at 10-15 fps. Get it from the Spriterrific/ChatGPT reference sheet, or from the Dead Cells route (Tripo model, Blender rig, low-res frames plus normals).
Gameplay-layer protection: the 9 playable columns are never blurred, fogged, dithered, bloomed or chromatically shifted. Atmosphere lives only in the sky, the walls, the background and empty space.

Block palette discipline: 4 block colors per level with clearly separated luminance. Run a grayscale debug view as a CI-style check for every skin. Add a per-color glyph or face for redundant coding, keep block hues out of the environment palette, and offer a colorblind swap.
Ambient floor: the block shader clamps max(lit, albedo * floor) so hues stay identifiable at any depth, plus a thin emissive edge so shapes read in the dark.
Falling-hazard telegraph stack on top of position jitter: emissive pulse that speeds up, crack decal after 50%, frost-dust drip from the seam, and a danger shadow on the cells and hero below.
Replace ACES with Neutral or NoToneMapping plus one final LUT/grade per 100 m depth band, interpolated on camera depth. Grade the environment harder than the blocks.

Post budget: scene render (optional MRT for ID), at most one half- or quarter-res effect (bloom or lightmap), and ONE merged composite pass (outline, grade, vignette, grain, blue-noise dither). Add a 2-tier quality switch, cap pixelRatio, and default shadow mapSize to 512 on low tier.

Juice kit with a settings toggle: trauma-squared camera shake (default 50%, never on the column the player reads), 2-4 frame hit-stop on big pops, block landing squash, and shard particles in the popped chunk's color.

options.name: Ink & Gouache Storybook
options.one_liner: Flat-cartoon Yorkie and toon ice blocks drawn by the same ink pen, on a painted night-and-cave storybook page.
options.hero_art: Flat cartoon sprite with bold outlines, regenerated flat-lit with one shadow tone and an ink width fixed at about 3 px for the final on-screen height of about 1.3 cells, so it matches the world outline pass. Pure front view for idle only: add 3/4 side walk and dig frames, plus split head and body cards a few mm apart so the head bobs. The plane is subdivided 4x8 for a vertex-shader bend (ear and hoodie wobble, squash from hop/land values). Lighting is the shared 2-tone toon function, with a fake puffy normal from the alpha distance field so the left and right halves band differently, plus an alpha-offset rim (cool aurora rim above, warm lamp rim on the lamp side).
world_rendering: Ortho or 12 deg FOV camera; blocks are toon cubes with a 2-tone hue-shifted ramp (cool, saturated shadow per color, not darker gray).
Screen-space chunk-ID plus depth outline at a constant 3-4 px in warm near-black. Inner creases at lower weight. Hero ID gives it the same line.
Celeste-style chunk perimeter: lit top-left bevel and darker bottom lip only on exposed chunk edges, with random snow caps on up-facing edges.
Painted parallax cave cards (ChatGPT image under the same ink and palette rules) at 2-3 depths, and dark icicle silhouettes in the foreground at the screen edges.
Background outlines fade and tint toward fog color with depth (Sable); active blocks stay full-contrast.
lighting_and_post: Hemisphere and directional lights stay; the warm headlamp point light is the second key.
One merged final pass: outline, LUT grade per 100 m band, paper-grain multiply locked to the shaft (scrolls with camera Y), light vignette.
Line wobble from Heckel's displacement at very low amplitude, for a hand-drawn feel without breaking chunk edges.
Bloom only on capsules and pops, at quarter res on the high tier only.
options.palette_and_value_plan: Night sky indigo to violet with a muted green-violet aurora at the surface; depth bands go teal, cyan ice, deep indigo. Background sits in a mid-to-low value, low-saturation band that the blocks never enter. 4 block hues with separated luminance (pale cyan, gold, magenta, deep teal) plus glyphs. Ink is warm near-black (not pure black), and shadows are hue-shifted toward blue-violet. The hero's light-blue hoodie is the brightest cool note, and the headlamp amber is the only warm one.
readability_safeguards: Chunk-perimeter ink makes merged shapes the strongest graphic element.
Paper grain is under 8% opacity and masked off block cores.
Background outlines fade; active-block outlines never do.
Grayscale check per depth band LUT.
Wobbling blocks pulse emissive plus crack decal.
implementation_steps: Switch to the ortho camera; replace ACES with Neutral.
Write the custom 2-tone toon ShaderMaterial (lights:true, UniformsLib.lights) with a per-color shadow-tint uniform array and Roystan-style rim.
Add the MRT render target (count:2 plus DepthTexture); patch the block material to write the chunk ID (instanced attribute) to location 1, and the hero to write its ID.
Write a full-screen composite ShaderMaterial: 4-neighbor ID/depth edge, line color, fade by linear depth, paper grain, LUT, vignette.
Remove the inverted-hull meshes.
Regenerate the hero: flat-lit, fixed ink width, idle/walk/dig frames; build a UV flipbook; split head and body planes; vertex bend.
Add the alpha-offset rim uniform (screen-space light direction updated per frame).
Generate 3 parallax cave cards plus a foreground icicle atlas; recycle them vertically.
Author 5 .cube LUTs (or parametric uniforms) and crossfade them by depth.
options.biggest_risk: Line-weight consistency across AI-generated animation frames. If ChatGPT draws each frame with a different ink weight, the sprite flickers against the uniform world ink. Mitigate by generating frames large, then thresholding and re-stroking the outline in a build script, or by letting the outline pass draw the hero's outer silhouette and keeping only inner lines baked.
options.fixes_current_awkwardness_by: Making the world obey the sprite's drawing rules: same ink width in screen pixels, same tone count, same palette and same grade. The puppy stops looking like a different medium, and painted layers mean it is no longer the only drawn-looking thing on screen.

options.name: Frost Hi-Bit Diorama
options.one_liner: The whole frame (shaft, blocks, aurora and Yorkie) is rendered on one stable low-res pixel grid, t3ssel8r-style, with a locked ice palette and HD-2D-lite light on top.
options.hero_art: Pixel-art Yorkie about 24-30 px tall at 1 cell = 16-24 internal px. NearestFilter, no mipmaps, alphaTest 0.5, rendered into the same low-res target as the blocks, and position snapped to texels every frame. Squash and lean are quantized to whole-pixel steps (plus or minus 1-2 px) or separate frames, never continuous scaling. Frames come either from cleaning the ChatGPT pixel candidate into a sheet, or (preferred long-term) the Dead Cells route: Tripo puppy, Blender rig, orthographic AA-off renders at sprite size plus a normal pass, so the sprite gets 2-3 band toon lighting from the headlamp like the blocks. The hero gets the same 1 px ID outline as the blocks.
world_rendering: OrthographicCamera, tilted about 8 deg so block tops show a 2-3 px frosty lip. Internal target about 180-200 x 320-360 portrait, sized to integer pixels per cell.
Snap-then-offset smooth camera: round the camera Y to the texel, render into a target with 1 texel of margin, offset the blit by the error. Vertical scroll makes this trivial.
Sharp-bilinear upscale shader (fwidth plus smoothstep), replacing CSS image-rendering, so 1 px lines stay uniform on non-integer phone ratios.
1 px outlines from chunk-ID and depth at internal res, drawn as a darkened neighbor color rather than pure black. 1 px light glint on convex top-left edges.
3-band toon on blocks with a 16 px nearest frost texture; X-blocks get a distinct cracked stone texture with no glint.
Pooled snow and shard particles rendered at internal res, so they pixelate for free.
lighting_and_post: Stepped headlamp pool (core, mid ring, dithered edge) in the composite as a screen-space darkness term, plus one real point light for the toon response.
Bayer 4x4 ordered dither indexed by snapped world texel, only on fog, sky, aurora and the lamp falloff, masked off blocks and hero by the ID channel.
Palette lock: 32-color nearest-palette LUT strip at internal res, with 4 reserved block hues of 3 tones each.
HD-2D-lite: bloom from the emissive mask at internal res (capsules, aurora, stars, pops); background layers rendered to a separate low-res target and blurred (tilt-shift by layer, not depth DoF).
No real-time shadow map in this mode; stepped blob shadows for the hero and falling blocks.
options.palette_and_value_plan: A strict 32-color master palette: 8 night/ice environment ramps (navy, indigo, ice blue, cyan, snow white), 4 aurora accents (green, magenta), 3 lamp ambers, 12 reserved block tones (4 hues x light/mid/dark), plus ink and black. Celeste rule: every tile has a light edge, a mid body and a shared dark infill. Depth bands swap the environment ramps through the LUT; block tones never change.
readability_safeguards: 1 cell = an integer pixel count, so every block is exactly N px.
Dither is never applied to blocks or hero.
Reserved block hues are absent from the environment palette.
5x5 px glyph per block color.
Camera snapping removes shimmer while scrolling and during wobble.
Player-facing pixel-size setting (A Short Hike).
implementation_steps: OrthographicCamera plus a low-res WebGLRenderTarget (NearestFilter, antialias false); compute internal size from the integer pixels-per-cell and screen.
Implement snap-then-offset with a margin texel and restore the transform after render (port pixelAlignFrustum/pixelAlignObject from the three.js pixel example).
Write the composite ShaderMaterial at internal res: ID/depth 1 px edges with darkened neighbor color, convex glint, headlamp bands, Bayer dither masked by ID, palette LUT strip.
Write the sharp-bilinear upscale blit to the canvas.
Build-script the palette LUT (Node: .hex to a 32x32x32 strip).
Hero: downscale and palette-reduce the pixel candidate to the exact target height; make a flipbook atlas; snap to texels; quantize squash.
Optional L-effort follow-up: Blender headless script for Tripo puppy to frames plus normal-map atlas.
Emissive mask bloom at internal res; background layer target with blur.
Remove inverted hulls in this mode.
options.biggest_risk: Sprite pixel quality. AI 'pixel art' is usually fake pixels at an inconsistent grid. If the Yorkie isn't cleaned into true 1:1 pixels at the world's density with the locked palette, the hero reads as mushy next to crisp blocks. It needs a clean-up pass by hand or script, and ideally the Blender low-res render pipeline for frames.
options.fixes_current_awkwardness_by: Putting everything onto one grid and one palette by construction. Hero texels equal world texels, one 1 px ink is applied by the same pass to blocks and puppy, and ortho plus snapping removes the unstable perspective pixel mode. With identical resolution, ink and palette, nothing can look pasted on.

options.name: Lantern in the Deep
options.one_liner: A low-key, fog-and-silhouette ice cave where the puppy's amber headlamp is the world's key light. The direct Tidebreaker / INSIDE / Hollow Knight answer.
options.hero_art: Flat cartoon (or simplified flat-pixel) sprite rendered Ori-style as self-illuminated, not scene-lit, so it never gets muddy. A directional rim mask from alpha-offset sampling: warm amber on the lamp side, cool aurora cyan from above near the surface. It stays correct when the sprite flips. The sprite is slightly desaturated except the light-blue hoodie, which is the brightest cool shape on screen. A visible lamp source on the hood gets narrow bloom. The silhouette reads first, so pose clarity in frames matters more than interior detail.
world_rendering: Narrow-FOV or ortho camera; blocks keep toon shading but sit in near-darkness. A fake translucency term (Barré-Brisebois) against the headlamp only, so ice near the lamp glows through in its own hue and chunk edges glow (thickness attribute 1 at the perimeter).
Fresnel rim plus a thin emissive color edge on every block, so shapes read beyond the lamp radius.
3-4 parallax layers of near-black ice walls and stalactites with heavy depth fog whose color shifts per band (Ori custom fog).
Surface: a vertex-gradient night sky (Alto), a 2D FBM aurora curtain shader, twinkling Points stars, and fake additive light-shaft cones from the shaft opening that fade out below 50 m.
Breath-fog puffs from the puppy that grow as air runs low.
lighting_and_post: Screen-space lightmap at 1/4 res: additive radial blobs for the headlamp (radius shrinks per 100 m and with low air), capsule beacons, chain-pop flashes and an aurora band at the top. Composite as color *= max(ambientFloor, lightmap).
One real PointLight (headlamp) for toon response and translucency; no other dynamic lights.
Two glows: the wide glow comes from the lightmap, and the narrow glow is mip bloom with a high threshold on HDR emissives only.
Merged composite: vignette that tightens with depth and low air, blue-noise dither against banding in dark gradients, very light grain, chromatic aberration only as an event pulse on crush.
Turn it down 90%: muted environment, restrained VFX.
options.palette_and_value_plan: 80% of the frame sits in the bottom quarter of the value range (navy to blue-black). The only saturated elements are the 4 block hues (protected by the ambient floor and emissive edges), the amber lamp (the only warm color in the game besides chain flashes) and the hoodie blue. Per-band grade: surface aurora teal/violet, then cold cyan, deep blue, indigo, near-black, and a goal band with one new accent (geode gold, Gris-style reward).
readability_safeguards: Hard ambient floor so 4 hues stay separable at 500 m (tuned with the grayscale view).
Emissive chunk edges and glyphs visible outside the lamp.
Falling or wobbling blocks self-illuminate as they pulse, so danger is visible in darkness.
Fog and grade apply to environment layers only (fog:false on blocks).
Shrinking lamp radius is clamped so 3 rows below and 2 rows above the hero are always lit.
implementation_steps: Lightmap target plus a light scene of instanced radial-gradient quads (AdditiveBlending), rendered with the main camera at 1/4 res.
Block shader via onBeforeCompile: toon diffuse, then translucency term vs headlamp uniform, then fresnel and emissive edge, then the ambient-floor clamp.
Hero ShaderMaterial: unlit albedo plus alpha-offset rim with lightDir and rimColor uniforms from the active light context.
Parallax wall planes with a layer fog shader; per-band uniform table driving fog color, ambient floor, lamp radius and grade.
Aurora curtain shader, star Points, light-shaft cones.
pmndrs EffectPass: mip bloom plus lightmap multiply plus vignette plus dither plus noise in one pass; chromatic aberration gated by intensity > 0.
Breath and snow particle pools.
options.biggest_risk: Too dark to play fair. Deep bands can drop colors below discriminability, especially on dim phones or outdoors, and the mood then reads as murky rather than atmospheric. It needs disciplined ambient-floor tuning and the grayscale check per band.
options.fixes_current_awkwardness_by: Replacing 'two lighting models' with one light story. The puppy carries the key light instead of being lit by the scene, so the sprite is the cause of the lighting rather than a recipient that disagrees with it. Darkness hides the 2D/3D density mismatch, as fog and silhouettes did for INSIDE.

options.name: Papercraft Ice Diorama
options.one_liner: The bold option: stop fighting the 'sticker' and make it the aesthetic. A Paper Mario-style cardboard toy theatre where the puppy is a die-cut paper figure among cut-cardstock ice tiles.
options.hero_art: Flat cartoon sprite with an intentional white die-cut border (3-4 px at final size) and a subtle paper-fiber texture. It is a thin extruded card with visible edge thickness. Turning is a paper-flip (rotate Y through 90 deg in 80 ms and swap the frame), and hops are a paper bounce with a slight curl from a vertex bend. Lit with a mild 2-tone on the card plus a real alpha-cut cast shadow onto the cavity floor and the blocks behind, which is the key 'object on a stage' cue. The flat card is the whole point, so few frames are needed.
world_rendering: Blocks are thick cut-cardstock tiles: beveled paper edges with fiber grain (normal map baked in Blender from a beveled box), each color a different card stock. Merged chunks are one cut shape with a layered-paper edge.
Inner shaft walls are stacked paper layers with visible offset and drop shadows between them (cheap planes at small z offsets with AO).
Snow is paper confetti; pop shards are torn paper bits in the block color.
Aurora is translucent tissue-paper ribbons on wires, gently swaying, with light through them; stars are foil punches.
Slight perspective is acceptable here (diorama), but use a narrow FOV and a fixed camera.
lighting_and_post: Warm studio key from the top front plus a cool aurora fill; real shadow map (1024 high, 512 low) because cast shadows between paper layers are the look.
The headlamp is a small spotlight with a cookie as you go deeper; the stage gets dimmer, as if the lights were lowered.
Depth-masked tilt-shift only on the sky at the surface and the deep background layers, half-res separable blur.
Merged grade plus vignette; no paper grain overlay needed because the grain lives in the materials (world-locked by construction).
options.palette_and_value_plan: Craft-paper palette: off-white snow card, kraft-brown X-blocks (natural for frozen dirt), 4 saturated colored cardstocks for blocks with luminance separated, a midnight-blue construction-paper sky, translucent aurora tissue (green/magenta), and a gold-foil goal. Values stay mid to light at the surface and dim by 'stage lighting' with depth, but never past a floor, because paper must still read as paper.
readability_safeguards: Each color is also a different paper pattern (corrugated, dotted, striped, plain) for redundant coding.
Merged chunks are one cut silhouette with a thick edge, so shape reads instantly.
Cast shadows show the hero's position and falling blocks' landing spots.
Tilt-shift never touches the 9 columns.
Wobble reads as paper flutter plus edge lift, which is very visible.
implementation_steps: Blender headless: bake a beveled-card normal and AO map, a paper fiber tiling texture and 4 pattern masks.
Block material: MeshToonMaterial or 2-tone custom with normalMap plus pattern mask by color index; generate merged-chunk edge geometry, or fake it via the neighbor mask in the shader.
Hero: extruded thin box with the sprite on front and back faces, a white border added in a build script (alpha dilate), customDepthMaterial for cast shadows, flip animation.
Layered paper wall planes with AO and per-layer shadows.
Tissue aurora: alpha planes with vertex sway; foil star Points with sparkle.
Tilt-shift (Horizontal/VerticalTiltShiftShader at half res, depth-masked) plus grade and vignette pass.
Paper confetti and torn-shard particles.
options.biggest_risk: Theme dissonance. Paper and craft can undercut 'cold, frozen, deep, scary', and the ice-world mood the owner pictured (aurora night, dark cave) could turn into a cute craft table. Real shadow maps and tilt-shift also put the most load on low-end phones among these options.
options.fixes_current_awkwardness_by: Turning the flaw into the premise. A flat puppy in a 3D world looks wrong only when the world pretends he isn't flat. When the whole world is paper, the die-cut border, card thickness and cast shadow make flatness intentional and physically believable.

options.name: Frost Candy Arcade
options.one_liner: A loud, glossy, juice-first arcade look, DrillLand meets Puyo: jelly-ice blocks with faces, deep fake-refraction cores, and a pop and chain spectacle in the spirit of Tetris Effect.
options.hero_art: Flat cartoon sprite in a chunky early-2000s cartoon style (DrillLand's angular, bold, saturated look) with thick 4 px outline and a big readable silhouette. It gets a hard white specular sticker highlight on the hood that matches the block matcap highlight shape, so hero and blocks share the 'glossy toy' language. Self-lit with a colored rim. Animation is exaggerated: big anticipation squash before dig, overshoot on land, a dizzy frame when crushed.
world_rendering: Blocks are glossy ice-jelly blobs: rounded convex corners from the neighbor mask (rounded-box SDF clipped by neighbor bits), one bold perimeter outline per chunk.

Fake interior mapping: ray-box against an inner cube about 0.7 in local space for a darker parallax core with bubbles (64 px noise), fresnel rim, and a hard white matcap highlight baked in Blender. Single-pass, opaque, no transmission.
Each color has a Puyo-like face or carved glyph (snowflake, star, heart, drop); faces blink, and look worried while their chunk wobbles.
Per-100 m skin swaps (Meteos): snowfield candy, clear glacier with bubbles, aurora caverns with emissive rims, crystal geode facets, black ice. Same shader, different uniforms and matcap.
Bright, low-contrast painted background, kept simple so it never competes (Spelunky 2 lesson).
lighting_and_post: Mostly matcap plus emissive (cheap, consistent); one directional light for the blob shadow.
Threshold bloom (emissiveIntensity above 1 only) on capsules, pop flashes, chain counter and aurora; mip bloom half res.
Pop VFX: GPU-simulated shard InstancedMesh in the chunk color, a flash sweeping along the chunk outline, a snow puff; chains escalate with an aurora flare, camera kick and hit-stop.
Merged grade plus vignette; LUT per skin.
options.palette_and_value_plan: High-key and saturated: 4 jewel-candy block hues with strong luminance separation and glyphs, a pale pastel background (lavender night to mint ice) held one value step away from all block hues, white sparkle highlights, and black ink. Depth bands darken the background but keep candy colors at full saturation, so it stays cheerful to 500 m.
readability_safeguards: Faces and glyphs give redundant color coding; a colorblind palette swap is a uniform change.
Calm idle state (no idle sparkle on blocks); spectacle only on events (Tetris Effect excitation/relaxation).
Worried faces plus a fast pulse on wobble make the falling telegraph emotional and very readable.
Bloom is gated to HDR emissives so chunk edges never blur.
Grayscale check per skin (Lumines warning).
implementation_steps: CPU neighbor mask per cell as an instanced attribute on grid change.
Custom block ShaderMaterial: rounded-corner SDF from the mask, interior mapping core, fresnel, matcap sample, glyph or face atlas on the front face, emissive pulse from wobbleT.
Blender headless: bake 3-5 matcaps (one per skin) from a sphere.
ChatGPT image: face and glyph atlas, cleaned into a single-channel mask.
Shard InstancedMesh pool with spawn-time-driven vertex simulation; snow puff Points.
Juice controller: trauma shake, hit-stop timeScale, landing squash on block instances, chain escalation.
Skin table per 100 m: matcap, palette uniforms, background, LUT.
options.biggest_risk: Loses the moody ice-world atmosphere (aurora night, deeper and darker) that the owner described. It could read as a generic casual mobile puzzle game rather than a distinct world. Faces also add a strong tonal commitment that may compete with the puppy as the star.
options.fixes_current_awkwardness_by: Giving hero and world one shared material language (glossy cartoon toy with the same specular sticker and the same bold ink) instead of realistic lighting. Matcap-first shading means neither side is 'lit by the scene', so they can't disagree. The juice adds the feel that the static sprite currently lacks.
