synth.recommendation: Lead with B, Frost Hi-Bit Diorama, and borrow C's light story: the headlamp lightmap, shrinking radius, ambient floor, per-band grade and aurora spill. Of the five, B fixes the most items in the ranked diagnosis by construction. It puts one grid, one 1 px ink, one palette and one ortho projection on everything. It is also the cheapest on mobile because fill rate drops, and it tolerates AI-asset inconsistency best. It has a proven route to animation frames from our Tripo plus Blender toolchain (Dead Cells). C's lighting is what actually delivers the Tidebreaker-style 'feel' the owner admired: one warm key in a cold dark world. It costs little at low res and is style-agnostic, so it carries over if we change course. Runner-up is A, Ink & Gouache Storybook, if the owner's heart is with the flat-cartoon puppy. A has more charm and is closer to the character as drawn, but it carries real risk around ink consistency across AI frames and costs a bit more on mobile. D and E are deliberate contrasts. D is the bold reinvention, and E is the juice-first arcade answer. Show them as stills so the owner can calibrate taste, but I would not spike them first unless the owner reacts strongly. Whatever wins, ship the universal fixes first (ortho camera, one shading rule, chunk-ID ink, texel lock, grounding, minimum animation set). They account for most of the 'awkward' feeling on their own.
synth.spike_plan: Goal: the owner compares 3 looks in-game on the same scenario within about 3-4 agent days. (1) Day 0.5, shared foundation: land the universal fixes that every style needs (ortho camera, chunk-ID MRT target, neighbor-mask attribute, ambient floor, wobble telegraph attributes, Neutral tone mapping). Refactor the renderer behind a StylePreset interface { camera, blockMaterial(), heroMaterial(), composite passes, palette/LUT, lights, particlesSkin }, chosen with ?style=A|B|C and hot-swapped with keys 1/2/3 at runtime, so the game state stays identical across swaps. (2) Deterministic showcase: a fixed RNG seed plus a scripted 'demo reel' mode with debug teleports to 0 m (aurora surface), 150 m and 400 m. Each stop stages a wobbling chunk, a falling chunk over the hero, a 3-chain pop and an air capsule, so every style is judged on the same readability-critical moments. (3) Per-style minimum, about 1 day each. B: low-res target plus snap-offset plus 1 px ID edge plus palette LUT plus a cleaned 2-frame pixel puppy. C: lightmap blobs plus translucency term plus self-lit rim hero plus fog layers, reusing the current flat sprite. A: 2-tone hue-shift toon plus 3 px ID ink plus paper grain plus a flat-lit regenerated sprite. Skip hero frames beyond idle plus walk in the spike. D and E are shown as ChatGPT-image mood mockups composited over a real gameplay screenshot, not code. (4) Comparison artifacts: a Playwright script captures each style at each demo stop as a contact sheet (3 styles x 3 depths), plus a grayscale version of each to prove block readability, plus an FPS/GPU-ms overlay recorded on a mid-range Android and an iPhone via the quality tier toggle. (5) Owner review: play each style for 2 minutes on phone, score feel, readability and character fit 1-5, then pick one or a combination (for example B grid plus C light). Throw away the losing preset code; keep the foundation.

verdicts.strengths: It is closest to the character the owner actually drew and likes (flat cartoon). It applies one ink rule and one tone count to both the world and the hero, which is the correct cure for the 'sticker' look. The hue-shifted shadows per color and the Celeste-style exposed-edge bevel are good craft details. The painted parallax layers mean the puppy is no longer the only drawn thing on screen.
verdicts.weaknesses: It depends most on the weakest link in the pipeline: consistent multi-frame cartoon animation from ChatGPT. The biggest-risk note admits this, and 'threshold and re-stroke in a build script' is hand-waved. The 'fake puffy normal from the alpha distance field' plus the 2-tone toon applied to a flat-lit sprite is exactly the double-lighting problem diagnosis #1 complains about, brought back in. Line wobble is a gimmick that will make the precise chunk perimeters swim. Paper grain plus a LUT crossfade plus a full-res MRT outline makes three post features on mobile with no measured budget.
verdicts.readability_concern: Pale cyan is one of the 4 block hues, and the hero wears a light-blue hoodie in an ice world, so the hero will camouflage against cyan chunks. A constant 3-4 px ink on a 9-column portrait phone (about 40 px per cell) uses 15-20% of each cell's width as line and crowds small 1-cell chunks. Inner crease lines compete with the chunk perimeter, which is the one line that matters.

verdicts.strengths: It is coherent by construction: one grid, one palette, one 1 px ink, ortho projection and snapping. It is the most robust option for an AI-agent and AI-asset pipeline, because a 24-30 px sprite can be cleaned by script (downscale, palette quantize, hand-fix a few pixels), and frames at that size can be edited by the agent. It is genuinely cheap on mobile (the fill rate is tiny). Sharp-bilinear upscaling instead of CSS pixelated is the right call for non-integer DPRs. Reserving block hues out of the environment palette is excellent discipline.
verdicts.weaknesses: At about 24 px tall, the Yorkie's identity (hoodie and fur face) is at risk; it could read as a generic dog blob, and the owner cares about this character. A 32-color hard palette lock combined with the C-style darkness and a stepped headlamp will crush the dark ramps into banding and posterize the aurora. Do the palette lock before the light, or reserve more dark ramps. The '3D toon cubes rendered at low res' look is very close to the current awkward pixel mode, so its success depends entirely on execution details (snapping, 1 px edges, glints). The Dead Cells route (Tripo, Blender rig, frames) is L effort and lands in the spike as 'optional', yet the hero quality depends on it.
verdicts.readability_concern: A 1 px outline at internal res plus 3-band toon on 20 px cells reads well. The danger is that the dither and the lamp's darkness term bleed into empty cells next to blocks, so the ID mask must cover the hero and blocks exactly, with no 1 px halo. Also, 'hero 1.2-1.5 cells tall' (from the universal fixes) breaks pixel-grid gameplay legibility, because the hero overlaps the row above, which is where falling-block danger comes from.

verdicts.strengths: This is the actual emotional answer to 'make it feel like Tidebreaker': one warm key light in a cold world. Making the hero self-lit removes the lighting disagreement instead of patching it. The light story is style-agnostic and layers onto A or B. A lamp radius tied to air is diegetic UI, which is great design. The per-band uniform table is a clean architecture.
verdicts.weaknesses: A dark cave is what every moody pitch defaults to. For a puzzle game whose core is reading 4 colors, darkness fights the gameplay, and the 'ambient floor' clamp will end up so high that the mood is mostly vignette. The translucency, fresnel, emissive edge, lightmap and bloom stack on the blocks makes the gameplay layer the busiest-shaded thing on screen. That contradicts 'turn it down 90%' and the pitch's own gameplay-layer protection rule. 'Low' mobile risk is optimistic: a pmndrs mip bloom plus a quarter-res lightmap plus a full-screen EffectPass on a mid-range Android is medium. Darkness 'hiding' the 2D/3D mismatch is a band-aid at the surface level (0-50 m), where everything is lit.
verdicts.readability_concern: Phones viewed outdoors or at low brightness will lose the deep-band hues even with the floor. Breath-fog puffs and the hood-lamp bloom sit right on top of the hero and the cell directly above it, which is exactly where the player looks for falling blocks.

verdicts.strengths: It is a clever reframe: accept the flatness. The paper-flip turn needs far fewer frames, which really does solve the animation bottleneck. Using a pattern per color as redundant coding is strong for colorblind support. Real cast shadows make grounding trivial.
verdicts.weaknesses: It is off-brief: the owner asked for an ice world with an aurora night and a darkening cave, and papercraft reads as a craft table. Its 'ice' is all metaphor. It has the most asset-authoring load (normal and AO bakes, 4 pattern masks, layered walls, tissue aurora), the heaviest GPU (real shadow maps plus tilt-shift), and it keeps perspective, the very thing the diagnosis blamed. Confetti snow and torn paper on a dark background lose all frost.
verdicts.readability_concern: Patterns (corrugated, dotted, striped) on small cells add high-frequency noise that competes with hue. Cast shadows from the stacked paper layers darken neighboring blocks unevenly, so the same color reads as two shades.

verdicts.strengths: It is the most 'Mr. Driller' in spirit: DrillLand and Puyo are the genre's own visual language. Matcap-first shading is cheap and consistent, and nothing is scene-lit, so nothing can disagree. Worried faces on wobbling chunks are the single best falling-hazard telegraph in the whole pitch. Per-depth skin swaps (Meteos) give clear 100 m milestones. It also has the cleanest mobile performance profile.
verdicts.weaknesses: It throws away the owner's stated mood (night, aurora, deeper and darker), and the 'pastel background' contradicts the ice-cave descent. Faces on blocks compete with the puppy as the cute focal point. Interior mapping plus rounded-corner SDF discard plus a face atlas on every cell is not trivially cheap either. It is a lot of per-fragment work on a full-res portrait screen, though far less than shadows. It risks reading as a generic casual mobile clone.
verdicts.readability_concern: Glossy matcap highlights at the same position on every block create a repeating white-dot pattern that visually breaks chunk boundaries, because highlights can read as seams. Faces on every cell of a large merged chunk are noisy. Show the face once per chunk (at the centroid), not once per cell.

missing_ideas: Paint-over first, code later. Before any 3-4 day spike, take ONE current gameplay screenshot and have ChatGPT image restyle it in all 5 directions (plus the B+C and A+C hybrids). The owner picks in an hour. The pitch only does this for D and E; it should be the first gate for every option, and the winning still then becomes the art-direction target for the code.

Hero vs. world color conflict: a light-blue hoodie in an ice world camouflages the hero against cyan and ice blocks and frost. Either reserve light blue for the hero only (no block or environment use), or give the hero a permanent contrasting rim or outline color. Run a hero-on-every-block-color contrast check alongside the grayscale check.

Hero size must respect the gameplay grid. Mr. Driller's hero occupies one cell; the universal fix of '1.2-1.5 cells tall' makes the hero overlap the row above, which is where crush danger comes from, and blurs which column it is in. Keep the silhouette inside about 1 cell, letting only ears or a hood tip poke out, and make the head big (chibi proportions) so it reads at 1 cell.

Analytic outlines instead of MRT: the playfield is a known grid, so chunk perimeter lines, rounded corners, bevels and glints can be computed in the block fragment shader from a per-instance 4- or 8-neighbor bitmask (which the pitch already proposes for E). This needs no ID buffer and no edge-detect pass, gives exact constant-width lines, costs nothing on mobile, and works in any style. Reserve a screen-space ID/depth outline for the hero only, or bake the hero's outline into the sprite.

A 2D cutout rig (Spine-like) as an alternative to AI frame sequences for the flat-cartoon route: split the puppy into layered parts (head, ears, hood, torso, arms, legs, tail, drill) once, then animate procedurally in code. Cult of the Lamb, which the pitch cites, does exactly this. It removes frame-to-frame ink and identity drift, which is the stated biggest risk of option A.

Character identity at the target resolution: before committing to B, mock the Yorkie at the exact final pixel height on top of a real block grid and confirm it is still recognizably 'the owner's puppy'. If not, use a bigger head with fewer body pixels.

Make the HUD part of the style. The HUD is DOM: a pixel font and 9-slice frames for B, ink-bordered cards for A, a diegetic air gauge (lamp, breath) for C. A mismatched DOM HUD alone can make any style look pasted together.

A color-pipeline audit before any style work: check renderer.outputColorSpace, the sprite texture colorSpace, MeshBasic vs lit materials, and the 0.85 exposure under ACES. The current code mixes MeshBasic 3D spheres (eyes and nose at src/main3d.ts:239-249) and a Lambert sprite with toon blocks. Some of the 'awkwardness' is plain pipeline inconsistency that costs minutes, not a style.

Motion sells feel more than shading: dig-hit frames, block-hit flash and crack stages per X-block hit, landing dust, a held anticipation before falls, and audio. The pitch mentions juice but ranks shading higher; the owner's 'feel' complaint is likely half motion.

Define framing and the visible-rows budget: portrait vs. landscape, how many rows above the hero stay visible (to telegraph falls), and the safe area under the HUD. Lamp radius, fog and vignette choices must never cut into that budget.

Commercial and licensing note: Tripo free-tier outputs are public with no commercial use allowed. If the game might ever ship commercially, don't make the hero pipeline (the Dead Cells route) depend on free-tier Tripo assets.
corrections: Diagnosis #4 / universal fixes: 'pixel creep can only be solved under orthographic projection' is contradicted by the pitch's own reference. The Texel Splatting paper (arXiv 2603.14587) is explicitly about perspective-stable 3D pixel art. Ortho is the simplest solution, not the only one.

Diagnosis #3: inverted-hull outlines are not inherently world-unit. Extruding the hull in clip space (offset scaled by w) gives constant screen-pixel width. Also, in a near-flat ortho shaft, depth variation is negligible. The real flaws of the hull are inner seams between merged same-color cubes and the extra draw, not perspective width.

Option D: a customDepthMaterial is unnecessary for alpha-cut cast shadows. WebGLShadowMap's default depth material inherits map/alphaMap/alphaTest from the source material. Note also that a PointLight shadow uses customDistanceMaterial, not customDepthMaterial; the current code sets customDepthMaterial on the sprite (src/main3d.ts:311), which matters if the headlamp casts shadows.

Diagnosis #2 is confirmed and specific: pixel mode sets minFilter = NearestMipmapLinearFilter (src/main3d.ts:331), which still blends mip levels and softens the pixel sprite when minified. Use NearestFilter with generateMipmaps = false.

Universal fixes: 'alphaTest so it writes depth' is slightly off. An opaque material writes depth anyway; alphaTest just discards transparent texels so they don't occlude. The real fix is to drop transparent: true on the sprite (currently transparent plus alphaTest 0.5 at line 270), so it sorts and writes depth as opaque.

Option C: 'mobile_perf_risk: low' is understated. A pmndrs mip bloom plus a 1/4-res lightmap plus a full-screen merged effect plus a fake-SSS block shader is medium on mid-range Android at DPR 2+. B is the only option that is genuinely low.

Option A: hue-shifted 2-tone toon on a sprite that was regenerated as 'flat-lit' re-introduces scene lighting of painted art (diagnosis #1). Either light it with the shared function and no fake puffy normal, or leave it unlit and add a rim, not both.

Option B: 'snap-then-offset … vertical scroll makes this trivial' holds only for camera translation. The proposed 8-degree tilt needs the frustum-align approach from the three.js pixel example, and hero squash must still be quantized, as stated. That is fine, but it is not trivial with continuous wobble jitter on blocks, which must also be texel-snapped or it will shimmer.

Option B MRT/ID: with WebGL2 MSAA plus MRT, the ID attachment must not be resolved or antialiased, or the edges get garbage IDs. At low internal res, use antialias: false everywhere, as stated. For A, at full res, this pitfall is real and unmentioned.
critique.top_pick_and_why: I agree with B (Frost Hi-Bit Diorama) as the lead, borrowing C's light story in a restrained form, under three conditions. (1) Gate it with ChatGPT paint-overs of a real screenshot in all styles first, so the owner picks the feel from stills before any multi-day spike. (2) Prove that the Yorkie stays recognizable at the final pixel height (about 1 cell, chibi head) and give it a hero-only contrast color, because light blue vanishes in an ice world. (3) Draw block outlines analytically from the per-instance neighbor mask instead of an MRT edge pass. Why B: it is the only option where cohesion is guaranteed by construction rather than by artist discipline, which this team (an AI agent plus AI image tools) doesn't have. It is the only one that is truly low-risk on mobile. A 24-px sprite is the one hero asset an agent can actually clean, palette-lock and animate frame by frame without drifting from the drawing. C's single warm lamp supplies the Tidebreaker emotion on top of it, with the lamp radius doubling as the air gauge. Keep the 32-color lock flexible enough (more dark ramps) that the darkness doesn't band. If the owner's paint-over reaction favors the flat cartoon, switch to A+C, but build the hero as a cutout rig rather than AI frame sequences.
